bio.en: Keith Coleman and Jay Baxter lead Community Notes at X (formerly Twitter), the crowdsourced system that adds context and flags misleading posts across the platform.
bio.zh: 基思·科尔曼（Keith Coleman）和杰伊·巴克斯特（Jay Baxter）负责 X（原 Twitter）的 Community Notes 功能，这是一个通过众包方式为帖子补充背景、标记误导信息的系统。

summary.en: Keith and Jay explain how Community Notes works: anyone can propose a note, and notes are rated by people who have historically disagreed, which keeps them neutral and accurate. They insist all of humanity should be eligible to participate - including elites, advertisers, and government figures. Independent studies show notes genuinely shift users' agreement with misleading claims.
summary.zh: 基思和杰伊解释了 Community Notes 的运作方式：任何人都可以提议备注，而备注由历史上观点相左的人来评分，从而保持中立与准确。他们坚持认为全人类都应可参与——包括精英、广告主和政府人士。独立研究表明，这些备注确实能改变用户对误导内容的认同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The work that you guys do has had such a tremendous impact on the way the world works. I want to start with just giving people a brief understanding of what is Community Notes.

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: We actually look for agreement from people who have disagreed in the past. And what we see is when people actually have that sort of surprising agreement, that's what makes the notes so neutral and accurate and well- written, really, overall.
turns.zh: 我们实际上是在寻找那些过去曾意见相左的人之间的认同。我们发现，当人们确实达成了那种出人意料的共识时，正是这一点让这些注释如此中立、准确且措辞得当——整体而言确实是这样。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: One philosophical thing that's important is that we want all of humanity to participate and sometimes people are surprised by that. We have all of humanity. turns.zh: 有一个重要的理念是，我们希望全人类都能参与进来，有时人们会对此感到惊讶。我们面向的是全人类。这样一来，我们就有数据去了解哪些注释对真实的人类是有帮助的。每一条帖子都有资格被加注释。我们不应该把 Elon 排除在外，也不应该把政府官员排除在外。我们应该一视同仁……就连广告主也可能被加注释。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: There have been external studies run by people totally independent of us who have found that if you take a post with or without a Community Note, that actually people's agreement with the core claims in the post does change if they see it with a note versus without.
turns.zh: 有一些与我们完全无关的外部人士开展的研究发现，如果你拿一条带注释和不带注释的帖子对比，人们看到带注释与不带注释的版本时，对帖子中核心说法的认同程度确实会发生变化。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Community Notes is a way for the people, like the public, to add context to posts that might be misleading. The basic way it works is that someone on X can see a post. If they think it's misleading, they can propose a note that they think other people might find informative. Other people can then rate that note. And if the note is found helpful by people who normally disagree with each other, indicating that it's probably accurate, it's probably really neutrally-worded, it's probably informative, then it will show to everyone on X. The goal is just to get people more information about what they're seeing so they can make better decisions in their lives.
turns.zh: Community Notes 是一种让公众为可能具有误导性的帖子补充背景信息的方式。它的基本运作方式是：X 上的某个人看到一条帖子，如果认为它有误导性，就可以提议写一条他们认为其他人会觉得有信息价值的注释。然后其他人可以对这条注释进行评分。如果这条注释得到了那些通常彼此意见相左的人的一致认可——这表明它可能准确、措辞可能非常中立、可能很有信息价值——那么它就会展示给 X 上的所有人。目标只是让人们对所看到的内容获得更多信息，从而在生活中做出更好的决策。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter

I think people are often... If you said... turns.zh: 好的。我觉得很多没有真正深入细节的人存在一个关键误解，他们以为可能有人写了条注释就立刻显示出来，或者我们只是用多数投票来决定注释好不好。我认为这两种方式可能都会导致有偏见或不准确的注释。我觉得我们真正做的关键事情是，我们实际上是在寻找那些过去曾意见相左的人之间的认同。(00:07:48)：我们发现，当人们确实达成了那种出人意料的共识时，正是这一点让这些注释如此中立、准确且措辞得当——整体而言确实是这样。只是那些立场非常极化的人，在内容不准确时往往无法达成共识，对吧？我觉得这也带来了很好的防操纵特性。我觉得人们常常……如果你说……我想在 2020 年我们开始构建之前，关于这套东西到底能不能行得通，一群机器学习工程师可能会说“哦，你得把它做成闭源。人们会一直操纵它。你得用事实核查员提供的真实标签。没有外部标签你根本无法启动这套系统”。但事实证明，用这种我们称之为基于桥接的共识算法，是可以做到这一点的。

We cover those cases and I think that's an important distinction. We just have the philosophy that users should be able to make up their own minds, right? Like, "Here's extra context, take it or leave it," right?
turns.zh: 我想做一个区分，这也许显得吹毛求疵，但我认为很重要：Community Notes 是补充额外的背景信息，它并不一定是“事实核查”，对吧？所以有些情况下，帖子本身可能是真的，但也许只是因为有误导性，因为没有背景或缺少背景。我们覆盖这些情况，而我认为这是一个重要的区分。我们的理念就是用户应该能够自己做出判断，对吧？就像“这是额外的背景信息，接不接受随你”，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What I think about, you shared this with me, this example of a picture with a cat and somebody's Community Note was just, "That's a dog." Or is it the other way around or that's a-
turns.zh: 是的。我联想到的是，你之前跟我分享过这个例子：一张有猫的照片，有人写的社区注释就是“那是只狗”。还是说反了，那是——

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah. "A Palestinian boy shares his bread with a dog," was the post and it's a picture of this cat. So obviously, this particular note is not super necessary because it just says, "That's a cat," and links to a Wikipedia for cat. It's a good example that the system is... This is not something a professional fact-checker or whatever or you think would need fact-checking. But it's proof that the system is really run by the users at the end of the day and adds some comic relief, I guess. And the note is correct.
turns.zh: 是的。那条帖子是“一个巴勒斯坦男孩和一只狗分享他的面包”，而配图是一只猫。所以显然，这条特定的注释并不是特别必要，因为它只是说“那是只猫”，并附上了猫的维基百科链接。这是个好例子，说明这个系统……这不是专业事实核查员或任何你认为需要核查的东西，但它证明了这个系统归根结底是由用户运行，而且我想，它还增添了一点喜剧效果。而且这条注释是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. It's important.
turns.zh: 好的。这很重要。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When does a post get triggered to even be considered for Community Note? Is there a threshold or is it just you can write a Community Note on anything and people decide what they would vote on? How does that work?
turns.zh: 一条帖子什么时候会被触发、甚至被纳入考虑加 Community Note 的范围？是有门槛，还是说你可以在任何内容上写 Community Note、然后由人们决定投票什么？这到底是怎么运作的？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: So every post is eligible for notes and that was, again, another really important principle. It's like, "We shouldn't exempt Elon. We shouldn't exempt government figures. We should..." Everyone, even advertisers, can get notes. So any posts on the platform can get a note. And if you look in practice, you'll see notes appearing on world leaders, on Elon, on ads, on media organizations, and on, obviously, just regular people using social media. But yeah, the idea is really that it's an even playing field. For a note to be proposed, the person proposing it has to have earned the ability to write notes. So there is that aspect where you have to earn in to be able to do this. And the way you earn that ability is through your ratings by demonstrating the ability to help identify notes that are found helpful to a broad range of people. So basically, if you have an ability to see and know, recognize what's helpful with a lot of people, then you have the ability to start proposing notes.
turns.zh: 所以每一条帖子都有资格被加注释，这又是一个非常重要的原则。就像“我们不应该把 Elon 排除在外，不应该把政府官员排除在外，应该……”每个人，就连广告主，都可能被加注释。所以平台上的任何帖子都可能被加注释。如果你实际去看，你会看到注释出现在世界领导人、Elon、广告、媒体机构身上，当然还有只是使用社交媒体的普通人。但没错，核心思想是这真的是一个公平的竞争环境。要提出一条注释，提出者必须先赢得写注释的资格。所以这里有这个环节——你必须先“赢得”才能做这件事。而你赢得这种资格的方式，是通过你的评分记录，证明自己有能力帮助识别那些对广大人群有用的注释。所以基本上，如果你有能力看到并识别出对很多人有用的东西，你就有了开始提议写注释的资格。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually signed up to be on... What do you call these people? Note take-
turns.zh: 我其实报名成为了……你们管这些人叫什么？注释写——

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Contributors.
turns.zh: 贡献者（contributors）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Contributors. Yeah. So I've been rating. I haven't achieved-
turns.zh: 好的。贡献者。是的。所以我一直在做评分。我还没达到——

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can't write notes yet.
turns.zh: 我还没法写注释。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. It's not super easy. It takes some effort.
turns.zh: 是的。这不太容易。需要花点功夫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there stats you can share about the scale of Community Notes at this point, especially things that might surprise people?
turns.zh: 你能分享一些关于 Community Notes 目前规模的数据吗？尤其是那些可能让人感到意外的内容。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, the service is growing rapidly, so there are hundreds of notes per day. And to put that into context, I saw some stats recently from someone at UC Berkeley saying there was something like 10 traditional fact checks a day. So in contrast, there's hundreds of notes a day that are getting shown. They span a huge range of topics from, obviously, politics, news, out to entertainment, sports, gaming. Just whatever is going on that day. (00:14:07): In addition to there being hundreds of these individual notes, they can also be matched to multiple posts. So if someone writes a note on an image or a video, like let's say it's AI generated or something like that, that note will automatically be matched to all posts that contain the same image. So you can have a single note matching to thousands of posts. And over let's say the last year, 2024, we had something like 95,000 notes that were seen about 30 billion times. That's more than double the prior year. Prior year was something like 37K notes seen 14 billion times. So that rate is increasing dramatically when you think about 30 billion views, that's a lot of information that is getting out there that might not have been out there otherwise, which is pretty cool. And part of the reason it is expanding like that is the contributor base is expanding. There's something like 950,000 contributors around the world. That's nearing a million people making this happen which is amazing.
turns.zh: 好的。我的意思是，这个服务正在快速增长，所以每天有数百条注释。作为对比，我最近看到 UC Berkeley 某位人士的一些统计数据，说传统的事实核查每天大约只有 10 条。相比之下，每天有数百条注释被展示出来。它们涵盖从政治、新闻到娱乐、体育、游戏等极其广泛的主题，就是当天发生的任何事。(00:14:07)：除了有数百条这样的独立注释，它们还可以匹配到多条帖子。所以如果有人就一张图片或一段视频写了注释——比如说是 AI 生成的——那么这条注释就会自动匹配到所有包含相同图片的帖子。所以一条注释可以匹配到数千条帖子。而在过去一年，也就是 2024 年，我们大约有 9.5 万条注释，被看到的次数约 300 亿次。这比前一年翻了一倍多。前一年大约是 3.7 万条注释被看到 140 亿次。所以当你想到 300 亿次浏览时，这个速度在急剧上升，那是有大量信息被传播出去，而这些信息原本可能不会被传播，这相当酷。它之所以这样扩张，部分原因是贡献者群体在扩大。全球大约有 95 万名贡献者。这接近一百万人让这件事得以发生，令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. And I'm one of those, right? I count as a contributor?
turns.zh: 哇。而我是其中之一，对吧？我也算一个贡献者？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. Yep. No. If you're signed up as a contributor, you count.
turns.zh: 是的。对。如果你报名成为贡献者，你就算。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Cool.
turns.zh: 好的。酷。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Then, there's more people on the waitlist too. So there's plenty of headroom for more growth. Regarding the matching on media and URLs, I think that's a huge way to get extra coverage. Also, I do think we've been very careful to make sure that those matches are precise. Because I think one thing that people love about Community Notes compared to other types of fact checking is that, actually, the notes are custom written for the particular claim you're seeing, right? So often, a fact check warning would just say something like, "Get the facts here." And then, there's a link to some generic page about voting information, which is so not helpful to have the information behind a click. So pulling the context up so that you have zero clicks that you need to make and keeping it specific is so important.
turns.zh: 而且还有更多人在等候名单上。所以还有很大的增长空间。关于媒体和 URL 的匹配，我认为这是获得额外覆盖面的一个巨大方式。另外，我确实认为我们一直非常谨慎，确保这些匹配是精准的。因为我觉得，与其他类型的事实核查相比，人们喜欢 Community Notes 的一点就是，这些注释确实是针对你所看到的特定说法量身定制的，对吧？通常，一个事实核查警告只会说类似“点击此处获取事实”，然后链接到一个关于投票信息的通用页面，把信息藏在点击后面，这非常没有帮助。所以把背景信息提上来，让你无需任何点击，并且保持具体，这非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One feature I love that I imagine you guys thought deeply about is if I liked the post in the past, I get notified later if a community note shows up, so that I'm not remembering this false information.
turns.zh: 有一个我很喜欢的功能，我想你们肯定深入思考过：如果我过去给某条帖子点过赞，后来出现了社区注释，我就会收到通知，这样我就不会一直记着那些错误信息。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, we try to make notes as fast as we can, so we want them to appear instantly if possible. But inevitably, there's going to be a time gap between when a post goes live and when people figure out what's going on and when they get the note out there. And so, we send those notifications to try to close that gap. And yeah, we get a lot of love for that. We see people take screenshots and share them. They're excited about it. And it's also a pretty cool example of something you can do on the internet, in the social media world that was difficult in a print or standard news world where you would see maybe a correction the next day in a corner of a paper that was hard to read. Here, you're getting a ping about it if you've engaged with a post and note shows up.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，我们尽量让注释出得越快越好，所以希望它们能尽快出现。但不可避免地，在帖子上线、人们搞清楚状况、并把注释发出去之间会有一个时间差。所以我们发送这些通知，试图弥合这个时间差。是的，我们因此收到了很多好评。我们看到人们截图分享，他们对此很兴奋。而且这也是互联网、社交媒体世界里一件很酷的事——在纸质或标准新闻世界里这很难做到，你可能在报纸角落里第二天才看到一个小到难以辨认的更正。而在这里，如果你与某条帖子互动过，注释一出现你就会收到提醒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One user feedback point is I'd love the push to just tell me, "Here's what you got wrong." Because I find that I actually have to go into it and read it and I feel like the push could just be like, "Here's more context to this thing." You're like-
turns.zh: 一个用户反馈点是，我希望这个推送能直接告诉我“你搞错了什么”。因为我发现我实际上还得点进去读，我觉得推送可以直接说“这是关于这件事的更多背景信息”。你就——

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Agreed.
turns.zh: 同意。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: We'll go take a look at that-
turns.zh: 我们会去研究一下这个——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go. Live user feedback.
turns.zh: 这就对了。实时的用户反馈。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to get into the origin story of this whole thing. But two more questions, because we're on this thread. One is what's the the threshold for a note to show up on a note? Is that information you can share, just how does that work?
turns.zh: 好的。我想进入这个东西的起源故事。但还有两个问题，因为我们正聊到这个线索上。一个是，一条注释要出现，门槛是多少？这是你能分享的信息吗？到底是怎么运作的？

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: So just because of the details of the way the algorithm works, it uses this machine learning algorithm called Matrix factorization where we fit it with Gradient Descent and whatnot. The threshold is it's 0.4 on this made up scale-
turns.zh: 由于算法运作方式的细节，它使用的这个机器学习算法叫矩阵分解（Matrix factorization），我们用梯度下降等方法来拟合它。门槛是在这个人为设定的量表上达到 0.4——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 0.4. Great.

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, in practice, what it means is basically a majority of people... If there is a polarized divide relevant to the notes. Obviously, some notes are not about politics or something polarizing. But if there is, then a sizable majority of people on both sides would generally need to find the note helpful. And then, there are other rules that come into play beyond that main one. So even if it's above that threshold, it might get filtered out if... There's a separate algorithm that's looking at agreement between people's incorrect tags. So like maybe people found the note helpful but incorrect, right? It happens. And in those cases, it doesn't matter if it's above the helpfulness threshold.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，实践中，它基本上意味着大多数的人……如果与注释相关的存在极化分歧。显然，有些注释不涉及政治或极化话题。但如果有，那么两边相当多数的人通常都需要觉得这条注释有帮助。而且除了这个主要规则，还有其他规则会起作用。所以即使超过了那个门槛，如果……还有一个单独的算法在审视人们给错误标签之间的共识。比如也许人们觉得这条注释有帮助但内容不对，对吧？这种事会发生。而在这种情况下，它在有用性门槛之上也无所谓。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is probably the wrong way to think about it, but is it 40% of people that normally disagree, agree-
turns.zh: 我这么想可能不对，但它是说通常意见相左的人里有 40% 同意——

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. It's-
turns.zh: 好的。它是——

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: It means nothing like that. It's just like on some arbitrary scale-
turns.zh: 它完全不是那个意思。它只是某个任意量表上的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. If we change random other things about the algorithm, that number would also have to change to an equally seemingly arbitrary number. We arrived at some numbers like that by gauging user feedback. So we could share a lot of notes with people, get feedback on which ones are helpful, and just a line emerged about indicating where things go from questionable to pretty clearly helpful.
turns.zh: 是的。如果我们改变算法中其他随机的东西，那个数字也得变成另一个同样看起来任意的数字。我们通过衡量用户反馈得出了这样一些数字。所以我们可以把大量注释展示给人们，获取关于哪些有用的反馈，然后就会浮现出一条分界线，标明从“存疑”到“相当明显有用”的临界点。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah. And it is set right now, by the way, to be really conservative, I think. We just are pretty particular about quality and we really want note quality to be really high. I think Keith and I both believe that we live or die based on the quality of the notes at the end of the day. So we'd rather not show a note that maybe good, but we didn't have enough signal on than the other way around.
turns.zh: 是的。而且顺便说一下，我认为目前它的设定其实非常保守。我们对质量相当挑剔，真的很希望注释的质量能非常高。我觉得 Keith 和我都相信，归根结底，我们是靠注释的质量而存亡的。所以我们宁愿不展示一条也许不错、但我们信号不足的注释，也不愿反过来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes so much sense. I've never seen a Community Note that is wrong and breaking that promise is a big deal. So I completely get why you guys are super conservative there. Okay. Two more questions [inaudible 00:19:53] because I'm just curious. These weren't on my list of questions to ask, but I feel like people wonder this. How many notes are written versus end up showing up and triggering on a-
turns.zh: 这太讲得通了。我从未见过一条错误的 Community Note，而打破这个承诺是件大事。所以我完全理解你们为什么在那里如此保守。好。还有两个问题[听不清 00:19:53]，因为我就是很好奇。这些不在我原本要问的问题清单上，但我觉得人们会疑惑这个。写出来的注释有多少，最终又有多少会出现并触发——

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: We probably show about 8% of notes that get proposed. It's been between, let's say, 7% and 10% or 11%, something like that over time. The number can vary a little bit. And as Jay said, there are undoubtedly... And you can see it, there's clearly more good notes than we show, but the goal is to hold a really high bar. We want to show a note when it's going to be helpful, when it's not going to appear biased and undermine trust in the system. We want these to be neutral, informative, helpful. And as Jay was saying, we view the worst possible mistake as showing a bad note because that's going to undermine trust and the trust is why people like the product. (00:20:47): So yeah, the bar is there. And like I said, there's clearly some in that remaining, let's call it 90%, that are good. And then, there's a lot that are just not that great and there's some that are bad. And if you write one of these ones that are bad which bad being defined as people who normally disagree find the note not helpful, so it's like the inverse of the ones we show. If you write one that people normally disagree, find not helpful, you actually will ultimately lose your ability to write and have to earn it back. That other 90% is a mix. Sometimes people look at the number, they're like, "Oh, why don't you show more?" It's like, "Well, you probably actually don't really want us showing most of those." The gold here is that the system is able to filter out the good ones.
turns.zh: 我们大概只展示被提出来的注释中的约 8%。长期以来它一直在大约 7% 到 10% 或 11% 之间，大致如此。这个数字会有小幅波动。正如 Jay 所说，毫无疑问……而且你可以看到，明显有更多好的注释是我们没有展示的，但我们的目标是维持一个非常高的标准。我们希望在一条注释确实有帮助、不会出现偏见并损害系统信任的时候才展示它。我们希望这些注释中立、有信息价值、有帮助。正如 Jay 所说，我们认为最糟糕的错误就是展示一条糟糕的注释，因为那会损害信任，而人们喜欢这个产品正是因为它值得信任。(00:20:47)：所以是的，标准就在那里。就像我说的，在那剩下的（我们姑且称之为 90%）里，显然有一些是好的。同时，也有大量其实没那么好，还有一些是糟糕的。如果你写了其中一条糟糕的——糟糕的定义是，那些通常意见相左的人觉得这条注释没帮助，也就是与我们展示的注释正好相反。如果你写了一条那些通常意见相左的人觉得没帮助的东西，你实际上最终会失去写注释的资格，必须重新赢回来。那另外 90% 是混杂的。有时人们看到这个数字会说“哦，你们为什么不展示更多？”就像“嗯，你大概其实并不想让我们展示其中大部分”。这里的精髓在于，系统能够筛选出好的那些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense. Okay. One other question is there's many people that are very polarized, like very disagreeable with a lot of things. How do they filter into this algorithm? How do you deal with people that are super anti-vax, super Jan 6, like all these very extreme potential views?
turns.zh: 这讲得通。好的。另一个问题是，有很多人立场非常极化，对很多事情都极度不认同。他们是如何融入这套算法的？你们如何应对那些极度反疫苗、极度认同“1 月 6 日事件”等等这些非常极端的潜在观点的人？

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: If people really are so polarized that there isn't agreement among people that typically disagree, it's possible that this is one of those notes that might be correct, but it wouldn't be helpful to show as context. Maybe it's about a claim that people have really entrenched opinions about and they've read hundreds of things about it already. (00:22:15): Probably this is just not going to improve people's understanding. It's just not going to be a helpful user experience. So it might not be the worst thing in those cases to not show the note. People, a few years ago, were pretty pessimistic that maybe fact-checking never changes people's understandings about what's true. Actually, there have been external studies run by people totally independent of us who have found that if you take a community note or posts with or without a community note... That actually, people's agreement with the core claims in the post does change if they see it with the note versus without. So we are having an impact on this thing that people previously thought was maybe not so easy to do. (00:22:59): And so, it's nice to focus on the cases where there is the bridging agreement. I would also say there is this reputation component to the algorithm as well. So if you consistently rate notes in a way that is counter to the bridging-based consensus, then we will stop counting your ratings. So if you're the kind of person who constantly rates bad notes as helpful, we do filter you out. So there's a difference between those types of people versus the good but polarized ones.
turns.zh: 如果人们真的极化到在通常意见相左的人之间都无法达成共识，那么这可能就是那种也许正确、但作为背景信息展示出来却没帮助的注释之一。也许它涉及的是一个人们已有根深蒂固看法、并且已经读过几百篇相关内容的说法。(00:22:15)：大概这并不会提升人们的理解。它带来的用户体验就是没什么帮助。所以在那些情况下，不展示这条注释也许并不是最坏的事。几年前，人们相当悲观，认为事实核查可能永远无法改变人们对真相的理解。实际上，有一些与我们完全无关的外部人士开展的研究发现，如果你拿一条带社区注释和不带社区注释的帖子对比……人们看到带注释与不带注释的版本时，对帖子中核心说法的认同程度确实会发生变化。所以我们正在对一个人们此前认为也许没那么容易做到的事情产生影响。(00:22:59)：所以，聚焦在那些存在桥接共识的案例上是很好的。我还想说，算法里还有一个声誉成分。所以如果你持续以违背基于桥接的共识的方式去给注释评分，我们就会停止计算你的评分。所以如果你是那种一直把糟糕的注释评为有帮助的人，我们确实会把你过滤掉。所以这类型的人与那些虽然极化但并无恶意的人的区别在于此。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. I think one philosophical thing that's important is that we want all of humanity to participate. And sometimes, people are surprised by that. They'll be like, "Oh, aren't there people who shouldn't be doing this?", or like, "Their thinking is so extreme or something, maybe they shouldn't participate." But our view is it's actually we want to have all of humanity here. Because if we have all of humanity, we then have the data to understand what notes will be helpful to actual humanity. We can better model that better or better understand and better show those notes. (00:24:03): So it's advantageous to have people who have all sorts of points of views and we don't expect that every note will be loved by every single person. That's an impossible bar. But we do intend to show the notes that 80% of people are going to read and say, "Wow. I'm glad I knew that." And so, in that sense, it doesn't matter how maybe extreme someone views a person's views as. It's still great to have them in the program. So no matter what your views are, please sign up and participate. It helps identify what's really helpful.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得有一个重要的理念是，我们希望全人类都能参与。而有时人们会对此感到惊讶。他们会说“哦，难道没有哪些人不该做这件事吗？”，或者“他们的想法太极端了，也许他们不该参与”。但我们的观点是，我们实际上正是想要让全人类都在这里。因为如果我们拥有全人类，我们就有数据去了解哪些注释对真实的人类是有帮助的。我们能更好地建模、更好地理解和更好地展示那些注释。(00:24:03)：所以让持有各种观点的人参与进来是有利的，而且我们并不期望每条注释都会被每个人喜爱。那是不可能达到的标准。但我们确实打算展示那些 80% 的人读了会说“哇，我很高兴我知道了这一点”的注释。所以在那个意义上，某人对另一个人的观点有多极端并不重要。让他们参与进这个项目仍然很好。所以无论你的观点是什么，请报名参与。这有助于识别出什么是真正有帮助的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And we'll link to people if they want to actually sign up, so they know how to do this. Something we didn't actually specify, these are all volunteers. No one's getting paid to be doing these notes and voting, right?
turns.zh: 酷。我们到时会放链接，如果人们真的想报名，他们就知道怎么操作。有一件事我们其实没明确说明，这些都是志愿者。没有人因为写这些注释和投票而获得报酬，对吧？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. It's totally based on intrinsic motivation and we think that's a great reason to be doing it. When you talk to the most active contributors, a lot of them, they want to have better information out in the world and that's a great motivation. So yeah, that's why they... If you think about, like for these people, the impact they can have is nuts. So when we first launched US-wide, this was like in 2022, a note appeared on a White House tweet and the White House deleted the tweet and reissued an updated statement. (00:25:25): Imagine being the person who wrote that. You probably have 12 followers. Your posts probably get a couple likes. And here, you just put a note on the White House and they changed their public talking points based on what you did. That is an incredible amount of impact. So you could see why people are motivated to do it when they care about what's going on in the world. You don't have to be a big, well-known person to shape the discourse and information flow in a way that's helpful.
turns.zh: 是的。这完全基于内在动机，我们认为这是做这件事的一个很好的理由。当你和那些最活跃的贡献者聊时，他们中的很多人是希望世界上有更好的信息，而那是个很好的动机。所以是的，这就是为什么他们……如果你想想，对这些人来说，他们能造成的影响是疯狂的。所以当我们首次在全美推出时，那是在 2022 年，一条注释出现在一则白宫推文上，而白宫删除了那条推文并重发了一份更新后的声明。(00:25:25)：想象一下写那条注释的人。你大概只有 12 个粉丝。你的帖子大概只得到几个赞。而在这里，你只是给白宫加了一条注释，他们就根据你做的事改变了自己的公开说辞。那是一个难以置信的影响力。所以你能理解，当人们关心世界上正在发生的事时，为什么会受到激励去做这件事。你不必是一个有名的大人物，也能以有益的方式塑造讨论和信息流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's insane. There's so much to love about this. One is just the meritocracy of this whole operation of just anybody that is true and correct can participate and have impact. Also, it just shows you how much information we get that is just wrong. We had no idea how often we see things that are wrong and now we do.
turns.zh: 这太疯狂了。这里有很多值得喜欢的地方。其中之一就是整个运作的任人唯贤——任何真实且正确的人都可以参与并产生影响力。另外，它只是向你展示了我们接收到的错误信息有多少。我们此前完全不知道自己看到错误信息的频率有多高，而现在我们知道了。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Working on this product has made me realize just how many things I used to trust by default, that now I look at more skeptically.
turns.zh: 做这个产品让我意识到，曾有多少东西我是默认信任的，而现在我会更带着怀疑的眼光去看待它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Definitely mean these days. Okay. Before we get to the origin story, is there anything else along those lines you guys think might be really important to share, that are really interesting?
turns.zh: 在这个时代确实如此。好的。在我们进入起源故事之前，在那条线上，你们还有什么觉得非常重要、非常有趣、值得分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Sure. I guess one other thing is that although we don't actually use the fact that a post was noted in the core ranking algorithm, which we think is a nice property. There is a really big impact just organically, meaning not from the algorithm but just from user behavior, where people will like and re-share or quote posts way less when-
turns.zh: 当然。我想另一件事是，尽管我们实际上并没有在核心排序算法中使用“某条帖子被加了注释”这个事实——我们认为这是个很好的特性。但仅仅从自然（organic）的角度看，也就是不是来自算法，而是来自用户行为——它有着非常大的影响：当人们——

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Quote. Posts way less when notes are applied. I don't know, for people out there who typically run A-B tests on big platforms, you may already be familiar with this, but 1% is typically an awesome effect size for any algorithm change. We saw more like 30 to 40% engagement rate drops for likes and reposts in A-B tests we were ran when showing a post with or without a note, which is just crazy big. That's just an A-B test on the engagement rate, so that's not the network effect. If you capture the overall network effect of how post spread less by that person's repost, basically if you look top line with a difference in differences approach, multiple different external research groups have both found consistently that there's a 50 or 60% drop in total reposts, which is just nuts after a note is applied. It's having a really big impact on spread actually, too.
turns.zh: 引用（quote）。当有注释被加上时，人们点赞、转发或引用帖子的数量会大幅减少。我不知道，对于那些通常在大型平台上跑 A-B 测试的人，你可能已经熟悉这个，但 1% 通常就是任何算法改动都非常了不起的效应量了。我们在展示带注释和不带注释帖子的 A-B 测试里，看到点赞和转发的参与率下降了大约 30% 到 40%，这简直大得离谱。这只是参与度上的 A-B 测试，所以那还不包括网络效应。如果你把那个人转发导致帖子传播更少的总体网络效应也算进去——基本上如果你用双重差分（difference in differences）的方法看总数据，多个不同的外部研究小组都一致发现，总转发量下降了 50% 到 60%，这在该注释被加上之后简直疯狂。它实际上对传播也产生了非常大的影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so great to hear. It's what I would want to see and it's incredible impact. Basically, an AI image of something false would just go crazy on Twitter, and did before Community Notes came out, and now what you're saying is just adding that context, not actually... Like you're saying, the algorithm doesn't demote it. If there's something incorrect, it's just people are like, "Okay, this is false, why would I want to retweet this?" That makes sense.
turns.zh: 这听起来太棒了。这正是我想看到的，而且影响惊人。基本上，一张关于某件假事的 AI 图片会在 Twitter 上疯传，在 Community Notes 出现之前确实如此，而你现在说的是，仅仅补充了那个背景，并不是真的……就像你说的，算法并没有降权它。如果有不正确的东西，只是人们会想“好吧，这是假的，我为什么要转发这个？”这讲得通。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, the notes just totally take the wind out these stories. The thing will be going viral, note appears, resharing drops 50 to 60%, and that's it. At 50 to 60% per generation, the virality quickly goes to zero.
turns.zh: 是的，这些注释完全让这些故事泄了气。某个东西正在病毒式传播，注释一出现，转发量就掉 50% 到 60%，然后就结束了。以每一轮 50% 到 60% 的速度，病毒式传播很快归零。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: By the way, I have very mixed feelings about this next one, but authors become 80% more likely to decrease, sorry, to delete their post after they get noted, which okay, that's great, because less misinfo out there, but I'm pan about, because those are usually the best notes. If the note was so just good that you had no other option but to delete your post, those notes don't get seen by other people, right? Because-
turns.zh: 顺便说一下，对接下来这个我心情很复杂，但作者在被加注之后删除自己帖子的可能性会增加 80%——抱歉，是增加 80%——这好吧，因为这样错误信息就少了，但我感到遗憾，因为那些通常是最好的注释。如果一条注释好到让你别无选择只能删帖，那这些注释就不会被其他人看到了，对吧？因为——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's hard.
turns.zh: 那很难办。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: There's an argument, by the way, that seeing... Just because you might see the same misleading claim elsewhere off X, or somewhere else on X, it might be good to actually show... Better to have seen the post with the note than not see it at all.
turns.zh: 顺便说，有一个论点是：因为你可能看到同样的误导性说法出现在 X 之外，或 X 上的别处，所以其实展示出来……比起完全看不到，看到带注释的帖子反而更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Unsure about that claim.
turns.zh: 对那个说法不太确定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting.
turns.zh: 那太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I'd be so sad if I was that community note writer and just... Man, it's so good. They just can't even keep the post up. Okay. Coming back from today's world, where this small amount of code is changing the way people understand the world and what they believe, and making the White House rescind their announcements, zooming back to the beginning of how this whole project started, what I heard just briefly is, Keith, you were just tired of managing PMs, you wanted to just work on something yourself, you wanted to work on something impactful away from corporate BS, and you basically just started looking for something that was impactful, important, and you found this. Talk about just how it all came to be at the beginnings of the story.
turns.zh: 是的，如果我就是那个社区注释作者，结果只是……天哪，写得这么好。他们甚至连帖子都留不住。好的。回到今天的世界——这么一小段代码正在改变人们理解世界和相信什么的方式，并让白宫撤回他们的公告——再把镜头拉回到整个项目最初是如何开始的，我简要听到的版本是：Keith，你当时只是厌倦了管理 PM，你想自己单干，想做一些远离公司政治、有影响力的事，你基本上就开始寻找那些有影响力、重要的事情，然后找到了这个。说说这一切最初到底是怎么发生的吧。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, for me, the beginnings actually go back to why I joined, it was then, Twitter in 2016. I had a startup and we'd had some acquisition offers, and one of them was from this company, Twitter. It was 2016, it was the middle of the election between Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, and there were something like three televised debates, but every day, there was a debate happening on Twitter, and it was very clear, this is where people are talking about these things that matter, where information is being shared, where ideas are being formed. As a user, it was obvious that I could get good information there, but it was also obvious that there was questionable information floating around. I remember just looking, as an outsider, thinking like, "Wow, this is a really hard problem and it also seems really important," so we ended up going to Twitter and the company was in a turnaround at that point. (00:31:21): My first three years was just helping to get the company growing again, working on everything that was the consumer product, getting user growth going back and people wanting to work there again, et cetera, but a few years in, I was reflecting on what we had done. I think we had done a lot of good work getting momentum going, and people in the us and in the industry had tried things to deal with misleading information, but nothing was really working. It was obvious nothing was working. Nothing could handle the scale of the problem, nothing could handle the speed, and a lot of people just didn't trust the existing approaches. The existing approaches were either fact-checkers or internal trust and safety teams making decisions about what was or was not misleading. A lot of people just didn't want or trust that to be the way this was decided, which is very reasonable. (00:32:19): I'm looking at that, I was still managing a large PM team. That's a whole story in itself. That job required a lot of energy in, and I didn't feel like I always saw the output that I wanted to see from it. I didn't see the change in the product I wanted to see and I was contemplating, "Should I go start a company? Should I do something else?" And I kept coming back to this problem. I'm like, "Man, how is the world going to deal with this information quality issue of what we get on social media?" Wherever get it. I'm at this company where you can make a difference on this problem, why not go and try some crazy ideas and see if one of them might work? I had a kid, I came back from paternity leave, I went to my boss, Kayvon. I was like, "Hey, Kayvon. How about I just stop doing my job and I go work on this instead? 'This' being trying some crazy ideas to see if we can deal with misleading info." (00:33:24): He was stoked, so I went off and started working on that. It started with just reading any research I could on the problem and existing solutions. What was or was not working, what were the issues, and then into prototyping. Then it ultimately led to us building and piloting this idea that became Community Notes.
turns.zh: 好的。我的意思是，对我而言，开端其实要追溯到我为什么加入——当时叫 Twitter，在 2016 年。我当时有个创业公司，收到过一些收购要约，其中一家就是 Twitter。那是 2016 年，正值唐纳德·特朗普和希拉里·克林顿之间的大选中期，当时大约有三次电视辩论，但每一天，Twitter 上都在发生一场辩论，而且很明显，这就是人们谈论这些重要事情、分享信息、形成观点的地方。作为一个用户，我显然能在那里获得好的信息，但也显然有可疑的信息在流传。我记得作为一个局外人，看着心想“哇，这是个很难的问题，而且似乎很重要”，所以我们最终去了 Twitter，而当时公司正处于扭转颓势的阶段。(00:31:21)：我头三年就是帮忙让公司重新增长，做一切与消费端产品相关的事，让用户增长重新启动、让人们重新愿意在那里工作等等，但几年后，我反思我们所做的。我觉得我们做了很多好的工作让势头起来，美国国内和业内也都试过一些应对误导性信息的办法，但没什么真正奏效。很明显什么都没用。没有什么能处理这个问题的规模，没有什么能处理它的速度，而且很多人就是不信任既有的方法。既有的方法要么是事实核查员，要么是内部的信任与安全团队来决定什么有误导性、什么没有。很多人就是不愿意、也不信任用这种方式来做决定，这非常合理。(00:32:19)：看着这个，我当时还在管理一个很大的 PM 团队。这本身又是个故事。那份工作消耗了我很多精力，而我并不觉得总能看到我想要看到的产出。我没看到我想要的产品上的改变，于是我在想“我该去创业吗？我该做点别的吗？”而我不断回到这个问题上。我就像“天哪，这个世界要怎么应对我们在社交媒体上接收到的信息质量问题？”无论在哪里获取。我身处一家能在这个问题上有所作为的公司，为什么不试着去搞一些疯狂的想法，看看其中有没有能奏效的？我有了孩子，休完陪产假回来，去找我的老板 Kayvon。我说“嘿，Kayvon。我干脆不做现在的工作了，转而去搞这个怎么样？‘这个’就是试一些疯狂的想法，看看我们能不能应对误导性信息。”(00:33:24)：他很兴奋，于是我就离开去做那个了。一开始只是阅读我能找到的关于这个问题和现有解决方案的任何研究。什么有效、什么无效、问题在哪，然后进入原型设计。最终引导我们构建并试点了这个成为 Community Notes 的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I have so many questions and we're going to keep going through the story, but when you joined Twitter, what was the... It was called Twitter. At this point, I'm going to try to call it X now, which I know is important to your boss. What era of Twitter was it at that point? It was Kayvon joined and who was the CEO? Because there's been many.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我有一大堆问题，我们会继续把这个故事讲下去，但当你加入 Twitter 时，当时的……它叫 Twitter。这点上，我打算现在开始叫它 X，我知道这对你老板很重要。那是什么样的 Twitter 时代？Kayvon 加入的时候，CEO 是谁？因为换过很多任。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Okay, yeah. I came in December 2016, so Jack had relatively recently come back as CEO to turn the company around, and just to give you a sense of the state of the company, something like a third of employees were leaving every year. Just imagine a third of your team gone every year. The stock was in the toilet, the product was not really growing, so Jack was working on a turnaround and Kayvon was there already. Kayvon was running Periscope with a bunch of video stuff, and that group continued to... Jack was there up through the start of the Community Notes, then Birdwatch Project, and... Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的，是的。我是 2016 年 12 月进来的，所以 Jack 刚回来担任 CEO 不久，正着手扭转公司。给你一个公司状态的概念：每年大约有三分之一的员工离职。想象一下你团队里每年走掉三分之一人。股票一塌糊涂，产品几乎没有增长，所以 Jack 当时在做扭转，而 Kayvon 已经在那里了。Kayvon 当时在运营 Periscope 和一堆视频业务，那个团队后来继续……Jack 一直待到 Community Notes 以及 Birdwatch 项目启动之初，然后……是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, and it was called Birdwatch. I don't think we've used that term yet, but that's an important point. It was called Birdwatch initially.
turns.zh: 好的，它当时叫 Birdwatch。我觉得我们还没用过这个词，但这是个重要的点。它最初叫 Birdwatch。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. It was originally called Birdwatch when we started the project, but obviously, somewhat famously the name changed along the way.
turns.zh: 是的。我们启动项目时原名是 Birdwatch，但显然，颇为出名的是后来名字改了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, maybe let's just tell that story real quick, and I know we're zooming it forward, but just... I have this Twitter thread that I saw between Jack and Elon when they're debating what to call it, and Elon's like, "Birdwatch sounds creepy, I want to change it". Is there anything there you can share?
turns.zh: 是的，也许我们快速讲一下那个故事，我知道我们把时间快进了，但就是……我看到过 Jack 和 Elon 之间辩论该叫什么的 Twitter 推文串，Elon 说“Birdwatch 听起来很 creepy（诡异），我想改掉它”。那里有什么你能分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, the story there... The story, that's funny. Elon came in, acquired the company, and we had just launched the product relatively recently in the US. It had been in pilot for a year, but we had just made it available US-wide, and I guess he'd been seeing the notes. Soon after the exhibition, he DM'd me and he was like, "Hey, this Community Notes thing is awesome," and I was like, "I'm glad you like it, let's talk," so we talked the next day and he kept referring to it as "This Community Notes thing." I was like, "It's interesting you keep calling it that, because that's actually the very first thing that I called it." The very first figma mockup I made depicting this thing was called "Community Notes." I don't know why, it just felt really natural, so that's the first prototype we had tested. (00:36:14): Later, the project changed the same to Birdwatch, but Elon was like, "Hey, let's just call it that." The next day, we just changed the name. It's always notable for the team when you change the name, but really, the team was excited about it. I think it is a much more understandable name. Jack has made fun of it, calling it "The ultimate Facebook name," or something like that.
turns.zh: 是的，那里的故事……那个故事很好笑。Elon 进来，收购了公司，而我们刚刚在美国相对近期地发布了这个产品。它已经试点了一年，但我们刚刚让它全美可用，而我猜他一直在看这些注释。收购后不久，他给我发了 DM，说“嘿，这个 Community Notes 的东西太棒了”，我就像“很高兴你喜欢，我们聊聊”，所以我们第二天聊了，而他一直把它叫做“这个 Community Notes 的东西”。我就像“你一直这么叫挺有意思的，因为那其实是我最早叫它的名字”。我做的第一版 Figma 模型描绘这个东西时就叫“Community Notes”。我不知道为什么，就是觉得特别自然，所以那是我们测试的第一个原型。(00:36:14)：后来，项目把名字改成了 Birdwatch，但 Elon 说“嘿，我们就叫那个吧”。第二天，我们就改了名字。对团队来说改名总是值得注意的事，但说实话，团队对此很兴奋。我觉得这是个更容易理解的名字。Jack 还拿它开玩笑，叫它“终极 Facebook 名字”之类。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: The most boring Facebook name [inaudible 00:36:44].
turns.zh: 最无聊的 Facebook 名字[听不清 00:36:44]。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Boring name, which is funny, because they're now launching Community Notes. I think it is a very understandable, intuitive name, and I think it has served the product really well. There's a reason it was the name in the very first mockup.
turns.zh: 无聊的名字，这很好笑，因为他们现在正在推出 Community Notes。我觉得这是个非常好理解、直观的名字，而且我认为它对这个产品帮助很大。这是有原因的——它是第一版模型里的名字。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think descriptive names just makes sense. This connection with Elon, and I want to talk later about just how you've dealt with so many strong personalities over and kept this alive throughout so many changes, but before we get to that, you did something that I think a lot of product leaders, angel leaders, just people that have managed people dream of give up all this power, in air quotes, and career trajectory and influence and just, "Forget all that. I'm going to go back to just building something awesome, small team." Is there any advice there that you could share from that experience that you think might be helpful for other leaders to share or to hear to help them maybe do that same jump? Because that's really difficult in practice. Easy to talk about, hard to do.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得描述性的名字就是讲得通。这种与 Elon 的联系，我后面想聊聊你究竟是如何与这么多强势人物打交道、并在这么多变化中让这个项目存活下来的，但在那之前，你做了一件我觉得很多产品负责人、天使（领导）人、总之那些管理过团队的人梦寐以求的事——放弃所有这些带引号的“权力”、职业轨迹和影响力，然后“去他的，我要回去只是做点很酷的东西，小团队”。你从那段经历中能分享什么建议吗？你觉得可能对其他领导者有帮助、能帮助他们也许做同样跳跃的？因为这在实践中真的很难。说起来容易，做起来难。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, I think it is a difficult jump. I've done it a bunch of times in my career and I've always been very happy with it, where I started with a small team, that it grew into something bigger, and then I was like, "We're dealing with a lot of big production stuff, team's really big. I want to go back to doing something like crazy and new with a small team again." I've done that sawtooth leap a bunch of times, but it can be hard, because certainly, the natural... The classic career path is, I don't know, rewards or running a large organization or being a manager, or things like that, but I think, at the end of the day, you got to work on stuff you love, you got to be having fun, and I think people want to be having impact. (00:38:29): I think there's one myth that can get in people's ways. The idea that the more people you manage or the larger your scope is, the more impact you have. I definitely do not think that is true. I mean, look at Community Notes for example. If I had stayed running a large consumer PM team, what would I have produced? 16 more pages of OKRs? I don't know, a bunch of documents? I think building Community Notes has had way bigger impact on the world. It's become the industry standard for how to deal with this now, which is super cool. People love it, it's the first thing that is plausibly dealing with the internet-scale issue of information quality. I think it's unquestionably a bigger impact than I would've had if I were just doing whatever, doing some standard management track thing like I was doing before. I think that's true of so many other small companies and startups. Someone screenshotted I think it's Blake Scholl's LinkedIn the other day. He went from director of coupons or something to building the first supersonic-
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得这是个困难的跳跃。在我的职业生涯里我做过好几次，而且每次都很满意——我从一个小团队开始，它成长为一个更大的东西，然后我就像“我们在处理很多庞大的生产事务，团队真的很大了。我想再回到用一个小团队去做一些疯狂而新鲜的事。”我已经做过好几次这种锯齿状的跳跃了，但这可能很难，因为当然，自然的……经典的职业路径我不知道，是奖励管理一个大型组织、或者当经理之类。但我觉得，归根结底，你得做你热爱的事，你得从中获得乐趣，而我觉得人们想要的是有影响力。(00:38:29)：我觉得有一个会阻碍人们的迷思：你管理的人越多、你的职权范围越大，你的影响力就越大。我绝对不认为那是真的。我的意思是，以 Community Notes 为例。如果我当时留下来管理一个庞大的消费端 PM 团队，我会产出什么？多 16 页 OKR？我不知道，一堆文档？我觉得打造 Community Notes 对世界的影响要大得多。它已经成为业界应对这个问题的标准做法，这超级酷。人们喜欢它，它是第一个看似能真正应对互联网规模的信息质量问题的方案。我认为它毫无疑问比我如果只做我之前做的那种标准管理轨道上的事要有更大的影响。我觉得对那么多其他小公司和创业公司来说也是如此。前几天有人截了我觉得是 Blake Scholl 的 LinkedIn。他从优惠券总监之类变成了打造第一架超音速——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, from Groupon.
turns.zh: 是的，从 Groupon 出来的。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Those stories are everywhere when you look, so I definitely have found that, for me, I love building hands-on, I love trying crazy new ideas. I love the zero-to-one experience. It's fun to scale things up too, and it can be fun to operate at scale, but this team is a good example of one that operates at a very large scale, but that is still very small.
turns.zh: 当你去看的时候，这类故事到处都是，所以我确实发现，对我而言，我喜欢亲自动手打造，喜欢尝试疯狂的新想法。我喜欢从零到一的经历。把东西做大也很有趣，在大规模下运营也可以很有趣，但这个团队就是一个很好的例子：一个在非常大规模下运营、却仍然非常小的团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think the way you guys operate is what more and more companies are trying to do, remove middle management layers, create small teams that just execute and build impact, just like Ics. Whenever I say IC, I have a comment on YouTube, where like, "What is IC?" I'm just going to explain, individual contributor, non-manager is when I say the word IC. Let me follow this thread, and when I asked people about how you set up the team to operate effectively and protect it initially, there's this term, "Thermal," that came up a lot. It was like a thermal team, if that's how you describe it.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得你们运作的方式正是越来越多公司想做的——去掉中层管理，创建直接执行、创造影响力的小团队，就像 IC（个人贡献者）一样。每次我说 IC，YouTube 上都有个评论问“IC 是什么？”我就解释一下，我说 IC 这个词时指的是 individual contributor，非管理者。让我顺着这条线，当我问人们你最初如何搭建团队让它高效运作并加以保护时，有个词“Thermal”经常出现。好像是个 thermal 团队，如果你们是这么描述的。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is thermal?
turns.zh: 什么是 thermal？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, so anyone who's worked in a larger company probably knows that things can get bureaucratic or bogged-down, decision-making can be slow. There's these large planning cycles, people can try to take someone from one team, move them to another at random arbitrary times that can disrupt a project, all sorts of things like that. Our company, this is a number of years ago when we started this project, we had a lot of founders in the company. Kayvon is an example of founder who is helping to run the company, and he had this idea, "Hey, why don't we create this program, call it Thermal, where we could have teams that were somewhat isolated from that." They could run through their own process, they would have one clear owner. The team would be entirely dedicated to that project and we would just repeatedly make funding decisions as to whether to continue the effort.
turns.zh: 是的，所以任何在较大公司工作过的人大概都知道，事情会变得官僚化或陷入泥潭，决策会很慢。有那些庞大的规划周期，人们可能在随机任意的时间把一个团队的人调到另一个团队，扰乱项目，诸如此类各种情况。我们公司，那是好几年前我们启动这个项目的时候，公司里有不少创始人。Kayvon 就是一位帮助运营公司的创始人，他有个想法“嘿，我们为什么不创立这个项目，叫它 Thermal（热气流），让团队能在某种程度上与之隔离开。他们可以走自己的流程，会有一个明确的负责人。团队会完全专注于那个项目，而我们只需反复地做资金决策，决定是否继续这个努力。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why was it called Thermal, by the way? What was the idea there?
turns.zh: 顺便说，为什么叫 Thermal？那个想法是什么？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: I think it was an old bird analogy of thermals lifting the bird on their wings. Twitter 1.0 obviously had a lot of bird analogies, bless its heart, so that was one of them. I loved the idea, as someone who liked the startup environment, so when we were starting this project, I was like, "Hey, Kayvon. Why don't we make this the first Thermal project?" And he was like, "Yeah, let's do it," so we started with that way of operating and it gave us, from day one, a lot of freedom and autonomy that I think was really important to make the product work.
turns.zh: 我想那是借用鸟乘着热气流（thermal）展翅升空的古老比喻。Twitter 1.0 显然有很多鸟的比喻，愿它安息，所以那是其中之一。作为一个喜欢创业环境的人，我很喜欢这个想法，所以当我们启动这个项目时，我说“嘿，Kayvon。我们为什么不把它做成第一个 Thermal 项目？”他说“好，就这么办”，于是我们就以那种运作方式开始了，而它从第一天起就给了我们很大的自由和自主权，我认为这对让产品成功非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just be very specific about it. What makes it a Thermal project? How do you set that up? This is asking from perspective, if a company wants to build their own something like this, what does that look like?
turns.zh: 具体一点。是什么让它成为一个 Thermal 项目？你是怎么搭建的？这是从一个角度在问：如果一家公司想打造他们自己类似的东西，那会是什么样？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, I think there's a bunch of key attributes. One key attribute is there's one clear driver of the project, who's effectively a founder. I guess maybe you could have two or something, but really clear, there's driver of the project and also there's one clear decision-maker that they go to.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得有一堆关键属性。一个关键属性是，项目有一个清晰的推动者，他实际上相当于一个创始人。我想也许可以是两个人什么的，但确实要清晰——项目有一个推动者，同时有一个清晰的、他们可以去找的决策者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Outside of the team?
turns.zh: 在团队之外？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Outside of the team. That was true back when we started and it is true now. If we need something or have a question about something, I talk to Elon. It was like that from the beginning, it's like that now, and I think that's a big reason we're able to make decisions effectively, quickly, in a simple way.
turns.zh: 在团队之外。我们刚开始时是那样，现在也是那样。如果我们需要什么，或对某件事有疑问，我去找 Elon。从一开始就是这样，现在也是，而我认为这是我们能够有效、快速、简单地做决策的一个很大原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It probably has to be someone very senior, not [inaudible 00:43:05] manager.
turns.zh: 那大概得是非常资深的人，而不是[听不清 00:43:05]经理。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Someone senior who can make the decisions you need made, whatever they are. I think that's really important, that clear decision-making structure. Another was 100% focus, so everyone on the project is expected to be totally focused on it. A lot of companies, it can be easy to have people's attention spread across a bunch of things, and it makes it hard to get stuff done. You'll talk to whoever that person is, you'll ask them for help on something, and they'll be like, "Yeah, I'll help you. I got to finish this thing, and it'll take me a week or two and then I'll get to it." A week or two delay totally changes the momentum of a project. When we were 100% focused, we talk in the morning, it's like, "Hey, Jay. Why don't we try this thing in the algorithm?" He's like, "Yeah." Then that afternoon or the next day, we're looking at results. (00:43:59): Because of that total focus, the rate of iteration goes way up. Then beyond that, there was also just the ability to use whatever our own decision-making process was. We didn't need to write OKRs or... For others standard practices. Obviously, we had to make sure we were responsibly building the product and everything, but we didn't need to use the standard practices. I think that's another great example, OKRs, I understand why they can be helpful, but they can also be not necessarily the right cadence at which to set goals. I think it's really unclear that quarterly or annual goals are actually the right pace. We would set the goal for the next milestone that mattered, and we would work on that. We reached that milestone, we would have an idea of what was coming after, and then when we hit that, we'd set the next milestone. Whether that was two weeks, a month, three months, whatever it was. We set our own pace and goals at that pace, and that just I think is a lot more natural for the development of something.
turns.zh: 一个能够做出你所需决策的资深人士，无论那些决策是什么。我觉得那真的很重要，那个清晰的决策结构。另一点是 100% 的专注，所以项目里的每个人都预期要完全专注于它。很多公司里，很容易让人们的注意力分散到一大堆事情上，这让事情很难推进。你会跟那个人聊，你请他帮忙做点什么，他会说“好，我帮你。我得先把这个做完，得花一两周然后我再弄”。这一两周的延误完全改变了项目的势头。当我们 100% 专注时，我们早上聊，就像“嘿，Jay。我们为什么不在算法里试这个？”他说“好”。然后那天下午或第二天，我们就在看结果了。(00:43:59)：因为那种完全的专注，迭代速度大大提升。除此之外，还有能力使用我们自己的任何决策流程。我们不需要写 OKR，或……对别人来说的标准做法。显然，我们必须确保负责任地打造产品等等，但我们不需要用标准做法。我觉得那是另一个很好的例子，OKR，我理解为什么它们可能有帮助，但它们也不一定是设定目标的正确节奏。我觉得季度或年度目标到底是不是正确的步调，真的很不清楚。我们会为下一个重要的里程碑设定目标，然后去攻克它。达到那个里程碑后，我们会对接下来要做的有些想法，然后当我们达成时，再设定下一个里程碑。无论那是两周、一个月、三个月，whatever。我们以那个节奏设定自己的步调和目标，而我觉得那对开发一个东西来说自然得多。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: The whole OKR determination and planning process took longer than it would take us to pick a goal and then execute on it and finish it.
turns.zh: 整个 OKR 确定和规划流程，花的时间比我们挑一个目标、然后执行并完成它还要长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How big was the team early on that you set up? How many engineers?
turns.zh: 你们早期搭建的团队有多大？多少工程师？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: It started with just me and then, when we decided to build the thing, we figured we needed about five. We wanted it to be as small as we possibly could. It was clear we needed someone on ML doing scoring, it was clear we needed someone to do some client engineering work, someone to do backend engineering work. There may have been one or two other. We needed a designer and a researcher to help us understand the customer base and make sure we were building the thing in a way that was actually going to resonate with people. I think it was backend, frontend, ML, design research. That was the original team, from what I remember.
turns.zh: 一开始只有我一个人，然后当我们决定要打造这个东西时，我们觉得大概需要五个人。我们想让它尽可能小。很明显我们需要一个做评分的 ML 人员，很明显我们需要一个做客户端工程的人、一个做后端工程的人。可能还有一两个别的。我们需要一个设计师和研究员，帮我们理解客户群，确保我们以真正能引起人们共鸣的方式打造东西。我记得最初的团队就是后端、前端、ML、设计研究。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Basically, one of each function. A question I have for Jay, actually, is there's all this talk of small teams and moving fast, but sometimes you just need more engineers to build the thing. Is there anything you've learned about just how to keep a team small while moving as fast as you are, and not need or need to hire more engineers?
turns.zh: 太棒了。基本上是每种职能一个。我其实有个问题想问 Jay：有这么多关于小团队和快速推进的讨论，但有时你就是需要更多工程师来打造东西。你有没有学到什么，关于如何在保持这么快速度的同时让团队保持小，而不需要或需要雇佣更多工程师？

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: I think, in the beginning when we were iterating on what should even the requirements be, it was definitely good to just have one ML engineer, but I think, at some point, we got clear on what the goals of the algorithm should really be and we tried... I think, at the very beginning, it wasn't clear that we needed to build this bridging-based algorithm. The actual first algorithm that I put into production was very focused on anti-manipulation. It was this page rank variant, but it didn't solve the problem of bias, basically. If there are more users on one side, a page rank type graph algorithm can actually amplify those biases. I think, after building that prototype and getting data from that, it was clear that the bridging-based algorithm was going to be the way that we needed to solve it, and at that point, basically I set up a bake-off. Kind of a Kaggle competition or something. That was the key time where it was really important to pull in other engineers.
turns.zh: 我觉得，在最初我们还在迭代到底该有什么要求时，只有一个 ML 工程师确实很好，但我想，到了某个节点，我们对算法真正该有的目标变清晰了，我们尝试……我觉得，最开始并不清楚我们需要打造这个基于桥接的算法。我投入生产环境的第一版实际算法非常聚焦于防操纵。它是 PageRank 的一个变体，但它基本上没解决偏见的问题。如果某一方的用户更多，PageRank 这类图算法实际上会放大那些偏见。我觉得，在打造那个原型并从中获得数据之后，很明显基于桥接的算法才是我们需要用来解决它的方式，而在那个节点，基本上我搞了一个内部比拼（bake-off）。有点像 Kaggle 竞赛之类的。那是真正重要的、需要拉进其他工程师的关键时刻。

turns.en: That is such a cool story. I want to follow that thread. Before we do that, you just mentioned you guys yell "Thermal." What does that mean? Is that YOLO, like a version of... Okay.
