I was going to ask just what inspired this actual algorithm, and you basically did an internal competition amongst ML engineers to see who had the most successful algorithm. Netflix-contest style, Kaggle style.
turns.zh: 好的。营销人，我知道你们喜欢[听不清 00:47:52]，所以让我直奔主题。Wix Studio 给你所需要的一切，让你能在一个地方按任何规模为任何客户提供服务。你的工作流可以是这样的：用动态页面和可复用资源毫不费力地扩展内容；用内置的营销集成（如 Meta、CAPI、Zapier、Google Ads 等）加速项目；用直观的设计工具、关联的追踪和分析工具（如 Google Analytics 和 Semrush）在几天而非几周内对落地页做 A-B 测试；无需手动设置的麻烦就能捕获关键业务事件；从统一仪表盘管理你所有客户的社交媒体和沟通，然后创建、排期并在他们所有渠道发布内容。如果你在做内容丰富的网站，Wix Studio 的无代码 CMS 让你无需碰设计就能构建和管理。当你准备做更多时，Wix Studio 与你一同成长。加上你自己的代码，用 Wix 自研的 API 创建自定义集成，或利用强大的原生业务解决方案。用 Wix Studio 驱动客户真正增长。前往 Wixstudio.com。(00:48:52)：好，回到这个算法，这其实非常有趣，因为我从没听过这些。我本来想问是什么启发了这套实际算法，而你们基本上是在 ML 工程师中搞了一场内部竞赛，看谁的算法最成功。Netflix 竞赛风格、Kaggle 风格。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. This particular idea of finding content that is liked by people on opposite sides of a polarized divider who typically disagree, this was not an idea out of thin air. I think Keith had found some of Chris Bale's work, he had made this list of accounts that were often liked by people who were on both sides politically. There is other projects, like polls out there that look for agreement among people who typically disagree, but I think that it wasn't obvious that our project definitely needed to use that from the very beginning. When you implement it and compare it against these other type... PageRank seems, obviously, it's designed to be manipulation-resistant. Naturally, if you just have a voting ring of people who all vote themselves up, then PageRank can filter that out very well, but that just wasn't the main attack vector, I guess. (00:50:15): We had to get some real data from the pilot to realize that, "Okay, the real thing going on here is people are polarized," so it was only once we got that, the real data from the pilot, that I think it was clear that the bridging-based algorithm was the direction we really needed to go.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。这个特定想法——去寻找被极化分界线两边、通常意见相左的人所共同喜欢的内容——并非凭空而来。我想 Keith 当时发现了 Chris Bale 的一些工作，他列过一个账号清单，这些账号常被政治立场两边的人都点赞。还有其他项目，比如一些投票项目，也在寻找通常意见相左的人之间的共识，但我觉得，我们的项目从一开始就必然要用到那个思路，这一点并不明显。当你实现它并与其他类型……PageRank 显然，它设计上就抗操纵。自然，如果你只有一个互相刷票的投票小圈子，PageRank 能很好地过滤掉，但我想那并不是主要的攻击向量。(00:50:15)：我们得从试点拿到一些真实数据才意识到“好，这里真正发生的是人们在极化”，所以只有当我们拿到那个——来自试点的真实数据——我才觉得很清楚，基于桥接的算法才是我们真正需要走的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to the way you operate the team. I hear that you run the whole team off a single Google Doc that's like a four-year-old doc that you just keep adding goals to, bullet points. Is that true?
turns.zh: 我想回到你们运作团队的方式。我听说你们整个团队只靠一个 Google 文档来运转，那是个四年前的文档，你们就一直往里加目标、加要点。是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: There is a very long-running doc that has had to be chopped and purged, because it was breaking Google Docs in Chrome at various points in time. It's like a note-taking doc. It's really where we coordinate what we're doing. The team meets on a daily basis, we spend whatever amount of time we need to get on the same page about what we're building. We might talk about anything from what's most important right now to, "What should we work on next?" To, "What are we trying to launch right now, and why is it not launched? What's in the way of launching it?" We might review new modeling or scoring algorithm update and try to understand what's working in it, what's not. We'll just cover whatever we want or whatever feels most important. As you said, we set our goals very dynamically, so whatever seems like the most important thing for us to work on now and next is what we spend our time on. I think that's served the project really well versus feeling attached to some quarterly goals, or something. We'll look at, "What is going to help people the most?" Or, "What's the biggest problem right now?" What are either one of those? And we will go tackle it. We might change our roadmap multiple times in two weeks based on what we see.
turns.zh: 有一个运行了很久的文档，中间不得不被裁剪和清理过，因为它在某些时间点上把 Chrome 里的 Google Docs 都搞崩了。它就像一个记笔记的文档。那真是我们协调在做什么的地方。团队每天开会，我们花所需的时间来对齐我们在打造什么。我们可能聊从“现在最重要的是什么”到“我们接下来该做什么？”到“我们现在想发布什么，为什么还没发布？是什么挡住了发布的路？”任何事。我们可能会评审新的建模或评分算法更新，试图理解里面什么有效、什么无效。我们就覆盖任何我们想聊的、或感觉最重要的。正如你说的，我们非常动态地设定目标，所以无论现在和接下来对我们最重要的事是什么，我们就把时间花在那上面。我觉得这比死守某些季度目标之类对我们项目帮助大得多。我们会看“什么最能帮助人们？”或“现在最大的问题是什么？”这两者之一，然后我们就去攻克它。基于我们看到的情况，我们可能两周内把路线图改好几次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm hearing no Jira, no Asana, no Monday.com.
turns.zh: 我听到的是：没有 Jira，没有 Asana，没有 Monday.com。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, we have to use Jira to coordinate with some other teams. Sometimes when we file a request, we have to make a Jira ticket. But no, I am not a fan of heavyweight task management. I love being on the same page, being able to keep most things in my head, and having a really light way to write down the things that the team can't keep in its head.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是，我们得用 Jira 来和别的团队协调。有时我们提一个需求，得开一个 Jira 工单。但并没有，我不喜欢重量级的任务管理。我喜欢保持对齐，能把大部分东西记在脑子里，并且有一个非常轻量的方式来记下团队脑子里装不下的东西。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: We did use Asana briefly, but my memory of it is that you spent more time in the meeting grooming a backlog of irrelevant stuff than actually talking about the proper priorities. I think it's nice in the Google Doc that, if something becomes irrelevant, it can just fall off without needing explicit backlog grooming.
turns.zh: 我们确实短暂用过 Asana，但我的记忆是，你在会议里花在梳理一堆不相关积压事项上的时间，比真正讨论正确优先级还多。我觉得 Google 文档好就好在，如果某件事变得不相关了，它可以就那么掉出去，而不需要明确的积压梳理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to maybe summarize a little bit of how you guys operate that might inspire other companies to set teams up like this, so I'm going to go through a few things you shared. One is one person in charge of the team, like the founder almost. They're basically the founder of the team. They have one very senior, essentially, sponsor/decision-maker that they interface with. In your case, Elon, no big deal. In other cases, it could be the CTO, CPO, someone like that. The team is focused 100% on its product and goal. You keep the team very small, so you start with one person of each function. One front-end engineer, back-end, ML person, designer, researcher, PM, and then Google Docs is almost basically for your project management. Yeah, it's basically run with Google Docs, stop, don't use big, complicated products.
turns.zh: 让我总结一下你们运作的方式，也许能启发别的公司这样搭建团队，所以我把你们分享的几点过一遍。一是团队由一个人负责，几乎像创始人。他们基本上就是团队的创始人。他们对接的是一个非常资深的、本质上是赞助者/决策者的人。在你们这 case 是 Elon，小意思。在别的 case，可能是 CTO、CPO，类似的人。团队 100% 专注于它的产品和目标。你们让团队非常小，所以你从每种职能一个人开始：一个前端工程师、后端、ML 人员、设计师、研究员、PM，然后 Google Docs 几乎就是你们的项目管理。是的，基本就是用 Google Docs 运作，打住，别用那些庞大复杂的产品。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: I think that's a pretty good recipe. On the Google Docs, people can do what they want. If they want to use thumbnails, go for it. I think those first ingredients, really, are key structurally. Then beyond that, it's a matter of having an ambitious goal that gets-
turns.zh: 我觉得那是个相当不错的配方。在 Google Docs 上，人们可以做他们想做的。如果他们想用缩略图，去用。我觉得那些最初的成分，真的是结构上的关键。除此之外，就是得有一个宏大的目标，能——

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: And then beyond that, it's a matter of having an ambitious goal that gets people fired up to go do great work.
turns.zh: 然后除此之外，就是得有一个能让人燃起来去做出出色工作的宏大目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Awesome. I think there's a lot there that a lot of people think they should do when they set these teams up, but they don't actually do, and it feels like each of these is just a really key ingredient to it to actually succeeding.
turns.zh: 是的。太棒了。我觉得很多人在搭建这种团队时认为他们应该做这些，但他们实际上没做，而看起来这里的每一条都只是真正成功的一个非常关键的元素。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: It definitely really helped us succeed. I don't know that the project would be here if it was not for some of those elements.
turns.zh: 它绝对真的帮我们成功了。我不知道如果没有其中某些元素，这个项目还会不会存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a powerful statement. This thing that has changed the way the world understands what is true would not have existed if you didn't set it up in this specific way.
turns.zh: 那是个有力的说法。这个改变了世界理解何为真相的方式的东西，如果你不是以这种特定方式搭建，就不会存在。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. I don't know if I would've begun the project had I not known. We had that structure, that ability to make decisions, the autonomy, the speed, the ability to go fast. We started with that in 1.0 and it's been continued and if anything, furthered in X. X as a whole company operates with a lot of those attributes, and I think it's one of the reasons the product is successful. I think those are big reasons why at least, Jay can speak for himself, I have so much fun working on this. I love working on it. It's great to wake up every day and solve these problems. We get to do them efficiently, make decisions quickly, build stuff that helps a lot of people. It's awesome.
turns.zh: 是的。我不知道如果我不知道有这种结构，我还会不会开始这个项目。我们有那种结构、那种决策能力、自主权、速度、快速推进的能力。我们从 1.0 就以那个开始，并一直延续，而且如果说有什么的话，在 X 里更进一步了。X 作为一个整体公司，是以很多这类属性运作的，而我认为这是产品成功的原因之一。我觉得那些是很大的原因，至少，Jay 可以自己说，我在这个项目上工作得这么开心。我喜欢做它。每天醒来去解决这些问题很棒。我们能高效地做这些，快速决策，打造帮助很多人的东西。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: This whether thermal or Elon way of operating is definitely more fun and the fact that... That combined with the awesome mission is super important for internal recruiting. I remember when I was first chatting to Keith about this back in early 2020, I had another project. I worked on a few, but one was like personalize the number of push notifications that we send, and it drove a lot of DAU without losing opt-outs significantly. So that was setting me on track, or if I had kept working on that, I could have probably gotten a promotion from that with low risk, or I could take this huge career... It's not as big at a career risk as joining or founding an actual external startup, but there is still career risk, I guess, in joining a team like this. I think all of the same aspects of recruiting that apply to external startups and apply internally, and if you can have an exciting vision, that is key.
turns.zh: 这套无论是 thermal 还是 Elon 式的运作方式，绝对更有趣，而且……再加上那个了不起的使命，对内部招聘超级重要。我记得 2020 年初我最早和 Keith 聊这个时，我还有另一个项目。我做过几个，但其中一个是个性化我们发送的推送通知数量，它在没有显著损失退订的情况下驱动了大量 DAU。所以那让我在轨道上，或者如果我继续做那个，我大概能以低风险从那升职，或者我可以冒这个巨大的职业……它不像加入或创办一个真正外部创业公司那样大的职业风险，但我想，加入这样一个团队还是有职业风险的。我觉得那些适用于外部创业公司的招聘因素，同样适用于内部，而如果你能有一个激动人心的愿景，那是关键。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Related to that and your list, Lenny, one thing we missed that's super important is that on this project, and I think of successful projects like it in startups, is that people are self-selecting to join. We did not assign anyone to this project. People reached out to join or they applied to join the job. I and the team interviewed every single person that joined the team and we were like, "We want that person on the team. They want to be on the team." And so people are totally bought in to the goal, mission, the way the team works, the other people they're going to be working with. And that makes a huge difference. (00:57:10): So a great time to do that is at the start of one of these things. If you're going to try something crazy, it's going to be tough if you're just assigning random people to it. But if you let people opt in and self-select much more likely to be successful. And one thing that I have observed at X, which really surprised me was that this is also possible at a large scale. One of the things that Elon did when he bought the company was he basically asked people to self-select to stay. You had to click the button. And he sent an email out that was like, "Hey, Twitter 2.0."
turns.zh: 与你那张清单相关，Lenny，我们漏掉一件超级重要的事：在这个项目上，以及我认为在创业公司里类似的成功项目上，人们是自我选择加入的。我们没有把任何人分配到这个项目。是人们主动联系要加入，或他们申请这个职位。我和团队面试了每一个加入团队的人，我们说“我们想要那个人在团队里。他们想进这个团队。”所以人们完全认同那个目标、使命、团队的工作方式、以及他们将要共事的他人。而这带来了巨大的不同。(00:57:10)：所以做这件事的好时机是这类事情刚开始时。如果你要尝试疯狂的事，只是随机派人去干，会很艰难。但如果你让人们主动选择加入、自我选择，成功的可能性就大得多。而我在 X 观察到的一件事，真的让我惊讶，就是这在大规模下也是可能的。Elon 收购公司时做的一件事，基本上是让人们自我选择是否留下。你得点击那个按钮。他发了一封邮件，大概说“嘿，Twitter 2.0。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fork in the road. Right? [inaudible 00:57:46]
turns.zh: “十字路口”（Fork in the road）。对吧？[听不清 00:57:46]

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Fork in the road. Fork in the road. Exactly. He's like, "Twitter 2.0, now X, it's going to be hardcore. We're going to do ambitious things. You're going to work your butt off." And you had to click on the form and say, "Yes, I want to join." And I think that was really important for the company because you want people to opt into that. You want the people to be saying, "Yeah, that's what I want to do," and the company's going to be a lot more successful. If people aren't sure, it's better for them probably to go do something else and where they're naturally more aligned and happier. And I thought that was a great approach to taking a large company and getting it down to people who are really excited about working together on a mission. So for us, we did it from day one, which I think is an easy way to do it, but it's possible to do it later as well.
turns.zh: “十字路口”。十字路口。没错。他就像“Twitter 2.0，现在是 X，将会非常硬核。我们要做有野心的事。你得拼尽全力。”而你得在那个表单上点击说“是的，我想加入。”而我认为那对公司非常重要，因为你想要人们主动选择加入。你想要人们说“是的，那就是我想做的”，而公司会成功得多。如果人们不确定，那他们大概最好去做点别的、他们天然更认同也更开心的事。而我觉得那是个很棒的方法，把一个大公司收敛到一群真的对一起为一个使命工作感到兴奋的人。对我们来说，我们从第一天就这么做，我觉得那是简单的做法，但后来再做也是可能的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you described it as fun and I think a lot of people when they see Elon laying off a bunch of people, being very hardcore himself, people don't imagine it as a fun place to work. And it's clear how much you guys love working on this, how fun it is and how interesting it is. And it's interesting to hear that 'cause I think a lot of people don't feel that externally. Is there anything else along the lines of just working for Elon within an org Elon runs that might surprise people about just the way of working that's interesting or surprising or you think other companies might want to think about adopting?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你把它描述成“有趣”，而我觉得很多人在看到 Elon 裁掉一大批人、自己非常硬核时，不会想象那是个有趣的工作场所。而你们有多爱做这个、它多有意思、多有趣，是非常明显的。听到这个很有意思，因为我觉得很多人在外部并不这么觉得。在 Elon 运营的组织里为 Elon 工作，还有什么其他方面可能让人感到意外——关于工作方式中有趣或意外、或你认为别的公司可能想考虑采纳的？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: I've always liked lean teams, but my experience at X has made me change the way I would think about running a future org-... If I were to start a company and had to change the way I think about starting that company, I would be even leaner than I would've made it before. I've been amazed with just how much the team is able to accomplish with a small group. And I think because of a small group, shortly after the acquisition, we had this product called Spaces. It had been in the product before, but it was pretty small scale, and Elon wanted to run these large spaces. I forget who the first people he was going to bring on were, but he was going to be there. Ultimately, these things have gone on to host politicians and things like that, and he's like, "Guys, we got to scale this up." I forget the numbers. (00:59:57): He's like, "We need to be able to scale a million people," or something like that. I'm getting the numbers wrong. "You need to be able to scale way up." This is the kind of thing at 1.0 That would've taken a year if it had ever happened, and the team did it in two or three weeks. And it was really exciting and inspiring to see. I didn't work on that, but I watched it from the outside. I'm like, "Wow, with this tiny team motivated behind a big goal that was like, 'Hey, guys, it's not like, are we going to do this?' It's, 'We are going to do this.'" They got it done in two or three weeks. That must've felt amazing for them. It was certainly exciting to see. But I've definitely come to appreciate just how lean something can be and not just get by but actually thrive because it's that lean.
turns.zh: 我一直喜欢精简的团队，但我在 X 的经历改变了我对运营未来组织……如果我要创立一家公司、并因此改变我对创立那家公司的方式的思考，我会比之前所做的还要精简。我一直惊叹于这个团队用这么小的规模能完成这么多事情。而我想正因为它小，在收购后不久，我们有个叫 Spaces 的产品。它之前就在产品里，但规模相当小，而 Elon 想运行这些大型 Spaces。我忘了他最初要带谁上来，但他会亲自在那。最终，这些东西后来承载了政客之类的人，而他说“兄弟们，我们得把它扩展上去”。我忘了具体数字。(00:59:57)：他就像“我们需要能扩展到一百万人”或类似的什么。我把数字记错了。“你们得能大幅扩展。”这类事在 1.0 时代如果真发生的话得花一年，而团队在两三周内就做到了。看到这个真的很令人兴奋和振奋。我没做那个，但我从外部看着。我就像“哇，这么一个小团队，被一个宏大的目标激励着，就像‘嘿，兄弟们，不是我们要不要做这个？’而是‘我们就是要做这个。’”他们在两三周内搞定了。那对他们来说一定感觉超棒。看到当然也令人兴奋。但我确实开始 appreciation，一个东西可以有多精简，不只是勉强维持而是真正繁荣，正是因为它精简。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the point you made about people opting into that is important, 'cause I think a lot of people hearing that would be like, "I would never want to be asked to build something like that in two weeks." And I think a lot of people do, and we love that kind of experience, especially working with the Elon, especially shipping something at that scale. But I think there's an important element there of just like, "Okay, I don't want to do that. I have other things to do in my life other than ship spaces." So I think that's a key point you've raised of just there's an opt-in step.
turns.zh: 我觉得你关于人们主动选择加入的观点很重要，因为我觉得很多听到这个的人会像“我绝不想被要求在两周内造出这种东西”。而我觉得很多人确实愿意，我们喜欢那种体验，尤其是和 Elon 一起、尤其是在那种规模下发布东西。但我觉得那里有一个重要元素，就是“好吧，我不想做那个。我生活中还有别的事，不只是发布 Spaces。”所以我觉得你提的关键点是，有一个主动选择加入的步骤。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Totally. I think the opt in is important, and it may even be that you want to opt in at one point in your life, and maybe at another point in your life something else is better. I think whatever it is you're choosing to do, it's nice to be opting in to feel like it's aligned with how you want to spend your time.
turns.zh: 完全对。我觉得主动选择加入很重要，而且甚至可能是你在人生的某个阶段想加入，而在另一个阶段别的事更好。我觉得无论你选择做什么，能主动选择加入、感觉它与你想花时间的方式一致，这就很好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something on my mind, and I don't know if you guys want to go here, but it's something I think a lot of people think about is when Elon came in, he let go of 80% of folks. And everyone's just like, "Twitter is dead. It's all going to fall apart. There's no way they can run this thing with that small of a staff," and clearly they were wrong. Clearly, it's working great. It's becoming a massive deal in the world and continues to grow. Is there anything about that that you were surprised by or anything about just how it continues to operate so well in spite of that big shift?
turns.zh: 我脑子里有个念头，不知道你们想不想聊这个，但我觉得很多人会想：当 Elon 进来时，他让 80% 的人走了。每个人都像“Twitter 完了。它会全盘崩溃。他们那么少的人手绝不可能运转这个东西”，而显然他们错了。显然，它运作得很好。它正在成为世界上的一个大事，并持续增长。关于那个，有什么让你惊讶的，或者关于它如何在大变动之后仍能运作得这么好，有什么想说的？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: I think the leaner team, the reduced process in bureaucracy is a big reason it does move as fast as it does. It's easier to get stuff done faster here. Yeah. I think that shrinking is actually a big reason for the increased pace of launches, the increased pace of experimentation. One thing that I noticed a result of that is the people who are here, they seem to all really feel like owners. They take the sense of responsibility that an owner takes in the product. They'll try to track down what's wrong, fix whatever is needed, jump in to help build or fix, improve any system that needs help, even if it's outside of their space. And there's the flip side of that too. For people who've worked at big companies, they may have experienced this thing where there's like ano-... You want to change something in some other system or product, and so you reach out to that team. And maybe they're a little resistant, they'll maybe be like, "Oh, we'll get to that next quarter or so-
turns.zh: 我觉得更精简的团队、减少的流程和官僚，是它之所以能这么快推进的一大原因。在这里更容易更快地完成事情。是的。我觉得那种收缩实际上正是发布速度加快、实验速度加快的一大原因。我注意到由此而来的一个结果是，留在这里的人，他们似乎都真的有一种主人的感觉。他们带着主人对产品的那种责任感。他们会去追查哪里错了，修复任何需要的，跳进去帮忙构建或修复，改进任何需要帮助的系统，即使那不在他们的领域里。而那也有另一面。在大公司工作过的人，也许经历过这种事：你想改某个别的系统或产品里的东西，于是你联系那个团队。也许他们有点抗拒，他们会像“哦，我们下个季度左右再弄那个——”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They have their own goals to hit. Yeah. [inaudible 01:03:08]
turns.zh: 他们有自己的目标要达成。是的。[听不清 01:03:08]

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. Exactly. They don't really necessarily want to help you or they're busy. Here, you're like, "Hey, guys, we need to do this thing with that other system you work on." And they're like, "Great! Here's the code. Here are the docs. Send us the fab if you have any questions, and we'll get it in." And it's just the thing, you can just jump in and get it done. And that kind of collaborative effort, like the sense of shared ownership, I think from my experience came from or was a result of the shrinking of the team down to people who wanted to be there and work together to build this thing. So I think that's been a really positive impact. It's not always easy. Certainly, a lot of people have a lot of responsibilities, but they're here because they're up for it.
turns.zh: 是的。没错。他们未必真的想帮你，或者他们很忙。在这里，你会像“嘿，兄弟们，我们得对你负责的那个系统做点事。”而他们会像“太好了！这是代码。这是文档。有问题发 fab 给我们，我们就把它弄进去。”而事情就是这样，你直接跳进去就搞定了。而那种协作努力，比如共享所有权的感觉，我觉得从我经验来看，来自于、或者是团队收缩到那些想留下来、想一起打造这个东西的人的结果。所以我觉得那是个非常正面的影响。这不总是容易的。当然，很多人有很重的责任，但他们在这里是因为他们愿意。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah. I think one other thing that's key is when you are forced to have such a small team, well, this is important anyways, but deleting code is more important than writing it a lot of the time. So I think so often maybe due to promotion incentives or just regular human tendency, engineers have a tendency to add these little incremental wins that actually add more of a long-term maintenance cost than is clear, because you just run a little one month A-B test, you see this significant win and you don't realize the maintenance burden you just added to your team for the rest of eternity until you turn the thing off. So I think there's a lot to be gained and you get forced to do this, by the way, when you have such a small team. It's just auditing parts of your system and deleting the things where the maintenance cost is worse than the gains. So I think we did have to do this across the company after the big layoffs, and systems are leaner now and they can be worked on by fewer numbers of people.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得另一件关键的事是，当你被迫只有这么小的团队时——好吧，这反正也重要——但很多时候，删代码比写代码更重要。所以我觉得往往可能是因为晋升激励，或者只是普通人的倾向，工程师有一种倾向去加这些小小的增量收益，而它们实际上带来的长期维护成本比表面看起来的要高，因为你只是跑了一个月的小 A-B 测试，你看到这个显著的收益，却没意识到你刚给团队加上的、在关掉它之前会一直存在的维护负担。所以我觉得这有很多可收获的，而且顺便说，当你团队这么小时，你被迫去做这个。就是审查你系统的一部分，删掉那些维护成本比收益还糟的东西。所以我觉得在大裁员之后，我们确实得在全公司做这个，而系统现在更精简了，能被更少的人维护。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing point. I remember Elon's being like, "Here, we have to throw away the whole thing. We have to re-architect everything. It's stupid the way it's built." And it sounds like that actually worked.
turns.zh: 那是个了不起的观点。我记得 Elon 当时像“这里，我们得把整个东西扔掉。我们得重新架构一切。它现在这个建造方式很蠢。”而听起来那真的奏效了。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah, so-
turns.zh: 是的，所以——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: You don't have to rewrite everything from scratch. Some things are good, I guess, to rewrite. But just even deleting the unnecessary cruft and keeping the rest of the core system, that's awesome.
turns.zh: 你不需要从零重写一切。有些东西重写是好的，我猜。但仅仅是删掉不必要的垃圾、保留核心系统的其余部分，那已经很棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that we're creating a formula to run these sorts of companies and teams. There's so much here. I want to go back to the building of the original product. I took us on a long tangent and an amazing tangent, but I heard a story of when you launched Birdwatch at that point. You specifically wanted to keep expectations very low and there was a GIF in the thing, and it just looked like clearly this is not ready for prime time. Talk about just how you did that, how you launched it in a way where people weren't like, "It's never going to work."
turns.zh: 我喜欢我们在创造一个运营这类公司和团队的公式。这里有太多东西了。我想回到最初产品的打造。我们跑题跑了好久，而且是个很棒的题外话，但我听到一个故事：当你当时发布 Birdwatch 时，你特别想让期望值保持很低，而且里面有个 GIF，看起来就明显“这还没准备好上主流”。说说你们是怎么做的、你们是怎么发布它、让人们没有像“这绝不可能行得通”那样反应。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: We were very disciplined, I guess you could say, about having the product prove itself at every given point. When we built the first mockups, these were just pictures of depicting what community notes might look like. We showed those to people across the political spectrum. We saw, hey, people really like these. Whether they're on the right or left, they seem very open to reading these community notes even when they're critical to people of their own side. So we're like, "All right. That gives us confidence that if we can build this, if we can actually make this as a reality, it's going to work." Then there's a question of can we make it a reality? Will people in the real world be able to write notes that are of this quality? (01:06:35): And so we had an internal pilot test version of this where you could write notes. And we first basically ran this through an Amazon MTurk type of participant test just to see if you just put some normal people in there, will they be able to write these notes? All those notes weren't good, but it was clear that there were people out there who could write good notes. So then like, "Okay, this is possible. What will happen if we actually do this out in the real world? And let's run a pilot and find out." And so we took that pilot that we'd run the MTurk of test on, and we released it to at first 1000 people, totally out in public, and we didn't know what was going to show up. You could imagine the notes could have been terrible. (01:07:27): And so we were talking, "Well, what do we do? We're going to put this out there. Everyone's going to have all these questions. They're probably going to be really skeptical, and we know it might be a total dumpster fire. And so what do we do to set expectations appropriately?" We felt like we could probably get there in the end, but we just didn't know what was going to happen at first. We wanted to set expectations, and so we're like, "Well, why don't we just stick..." There's the page where you see a post in the notes below. We're like, "Why don't we just stick a dumpster fire GIF on that page?" And you go there, you're like, "Hey, anything you see below here might just be a total dumpster fire. At least it would show we were aware of that as a possible risk." In the end, we did not do that. It cracked me up, but we thought it was like-
turns.zh: 我们在每个节点都让产品证明自己，你可以说我们非常有纪律。当我们做第一版模型时，那只是描绘社区注释可能长什么样的图。我们拿给政治光谱各方的人看。我们看到，嘿，人们真的很喜欢这些。无论他们是右派还是左派，他们似乎都很开放地去读这些社区注释，即使它们对自己一方的人持批评态度。所以我们就像“好。这给了我们信心：如果我们能把它造出来，如果它能成为现实，它会奏效。”然后有个问题是我们能把它变成现实吗？现实世界里的人能写出这种质量的注释吗？(01:06:35)：于是我们做了一个可以写注释的内部测试版。我们首先基本上通过一个 Amazon MTurk 类型的参与者测试来跑，只是为了看看如果你放一些普通人在里面，他们能写出这些注释吗？那些注释并不都好，但很明显是有能写出好注释的人。于是就像“好，这是可能的。如果我们真的在现实世界里做会怎样？我们来跑个试点看看。”于是我们把那个在 MTurk 上跑过的试点，发布给最初的 1000 个人，完全公开，而我们不知道会出现什么。你可以想象那些注释可能很糟糕。(01:07:27)：于是我们讨论“好，我们怎么办？我们要把这个放出去。大家会有一堆问题。他们大概会非常怀疑，而我们知道它可能完全是个灾难（dumpster fire）。那我们怎么适当地设定期望？”我们觉得最终大概能到那一步，但我们就是不知道一开始会发生什么。我们想设定期望，于是我们就像“好，我们为什么不就放……”有个页面，你在上面看到一条帖子，下面有注释。我们就像“我们为什么不就在这个页面上放一个‘垃圾桶着火’的 GIF？”你去了那里，就像“嘿，你在下面看到的任何东西可能就是彻头彻尾的灾难”。至少那能表明我们意识到这是个可能的风险。最后，我们没那么做。它把我逗乐了，但我们觉得它就像——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, you didn't actually launch. Okay. That was just a concept. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，你们其实没真发布。好的。那只是个概念。好的。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: We had mockups of it, and every time I looked at the mockup, I laughed, but ultimately we had so much to explain on that page, like, what is this thing and how does it work? Ultimately, we're like, "Okay, this is probably going to distract from the point." So we pulled it. I wish maybe it had seen the light of day at one point, but yeah, ultimately we kept it simple and we focused that page on explaining what was going on here. But again, as has happened many times with the project, we put the pilot out there and the notes were good. (01:08:48): They weren't all good. It was a mixed bag, but there was gold in there. And from the very early days with just 1000 contributors, it was obvious that people could write notes that were informative, that were neutral, that spoke to controversial challenging topics, and that if we could just identify those from the rest, this was going to work. It was going to work as well as the very first mockups we had made. So that became the focus that is, how do we sift out the gold from the rest?
turns.zh: 我们有它的模型，而每次我看那个模型都会笑，但最后那个页面上有太多要解释的，比如这是什么、它怎么运作？最后我们就像“好，这大概会偏离重点”。所以我们拿掉了。我倒是希望它某天能见光，但是的，最后我们保持简单，把那个页面聚焦在解释这里在发生什么。但再说一次，正如这个项目多次发生过的，我们把试点放出去，而那些注释是好的。(01:08:48)：它们不都好。是好坏混杂，但里面有金子。从最早的只有 1000 个贡献者时起，就很显然人们能写出有信息价值的、中立的、能谈论有争议的挑战性话题的注释，而如果我们能只是把它们从其余之中识别出来，这就会奏效。它会和我们最早做的模型一样好地奏效。所以这就成了焦点：我们怎么从其余之中筛出金子？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you may have shared with this with me, when someone noticed you guys were testing this and they took screenshots and tweeted it, and I think Elon replied, "This is cool."
turns.zh: 我觉得你可能跟我分享过，当时有人注意到你们在测试这个，他们截图发了推文，而我想 Elon 回复了“这很酷”。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. So in the very early days when it was just a Figma prototype, we were running these usertesting.com on moderated studies. I guess one of the participants sent one to an NBC reporter who wrote a bunch of stories on it. Anyway, that day, there was a lot of chatter about it on the service, and Elon... To put this back in time perspective, this is, I think, 2020, so two years before any acquisition stuff happened, Elon is just a Twitter user building rockets and electric cars and other cool stuff and stumbles on this thing that depicts the prototype that we've been testing. And he writes back, "Definitely worth trying, IMO." And I remember thinking that was cool back then and it's interesting to see, he's obviously had a very consistent point on it. I think the idea was appealing and he has obviously been a big fan of it in the product and had been a big supporter proponent. So yeah, it was cool that it came from... that support has been from the very early days before he was ever involved in the company.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。所以在很早的时候，当它还只是个 Figma 原型时，我们在 usertesting.com 上跑有主持的研究。我想其中一个参与者把它发给了 NBC 的一位记者，那位记者写了一系列关于它的报道。总之那天，这个服务上有很多人在讨论它，而 Elon……把时间往回放，我想那是 2020 年，所以在任何收购发生前两年，Elon 还只是个在造火箭、电动车和其他酷东西的 Twitter 用户，偶然撞见这个描绘我们一直在测试的模型的原型。他写回“绝对值得一试，IMO（依我之见）。”而我记得当时觉得那很酷，而且有意思的是，显然他对此一直有非常一致的观点。我觉得这个想法很吸引人，而他显然在产品里一直是它的忠实粉丝，并且一直是它的大力支持者和倡导者。所以是的，很酷的是，那份支持来自……来自他参与公司之前的很早的日子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that moment. That must have felt really wild for Elon to be commenting on this Figma prototype retesting.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个时刻。Elon 在评论这个正在重新测试的 Figma 原型，那对你们一定感觉非常疯狂。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: It was cool. It was cool.
turns.zh: 很酷。很酷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. So when we were preparing for this interview, I asked you guys what's the main thing you want to make sure people get and understand about why community notes has been so effective? And Keith, you specifically said that it was the principles behind how you wanted to approach this and how you continue to stick to this throughout. And we'll talk about how you kept it alive throughout all these different CO changes in leaders. But just talk about these principles, what the actual principles are and why that was so key to it working out.
turns.zh: 哦天哪。所以当我们准备这次采访时，我问你们俩，关于为什么社区注释这么有效，你们最想确保人们get到、理解到的是什么？而 Keith，你特别说到，是你们想用什么样的方式去approach这件事、以及你们如何持续坚守它背后的那些原则。我们会聊你们如何在这么多不同的领导层变动中让它存活下来。但先聊聊这些原则，实际的原则是什么，以及为什么它对成功这么关键。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: There are a number of principles that I think when we first shared them with people at the company seemed maybe a little bit crazy. But I think they are the reason the product works, and I think they've been very important, and we do. We come back to them regularly, today, all the time. Probably the craziest one is just that this thing is going to be the voice of the people. It's going to represent the voice of people. It's not going to represent the company's voice. So it is not a tech company deciding what shows. It is the people deciding what shows, and that had a lot of implications on the design. First of all, we don't have a button that will change the status of a note. So if a note is showing because the people have rated it and found it helpful, it is going to show. We can't change that. (01:12:08): And that is the kind of thing that when we first propose this, that's unsettling to people. They're like, "Wait, so something can go up and the company can't take it down, or can't change its status, get it to stop showing." And we're like, "Yeah, and it has to work that well. If it doesn't work well enough to do that, then it doesn't work." This is one of our key principles was, if there's a problem with a note that's so bad, you want to do something about it's a problem with the system. We need to redesign the system to be showing good notes. And so yeah, we had to get everyone comfortable with the idea that there was no button to change the status of a note. Similarly, as we talked about earlier, we wanted this to represent all of humanity. (01:12:53): And so we didn't want to be arbiters of who can come in and be a contributor and who can't. So we open it to everyone. You just have to meet a really basic objective criteria. You have to have a verified phone to help reduce the likelihood of having bots or things like that participating. But beyond that, it's random selection and it still is that way today. And again, that people took some time to get people comfortable with it. But I think that the fact that this is the voice of the people and reflects their output through an open and transparent process is so key to both why it is good, why it works, but also why it's trusted. So that's number one and I think will forever be the heart of the product. Another one that people thought was crazy was transparency. (01:13:49): The previous approaches to dealing with misleading info, it felt to a lot of people, like black box tech companies or media companies or leads or whatever making decisions. We're like, "People need to get comfortable with this. They need to trust this. So the whole thing has to be out in the open." The code that decides what notes share has to be out in the open. All of the data and ratings that make it happen have to be out in the open. People should be able to take the code and data and replicate the whole service and that we have done exactly what we've said we've done. And they should be able to audit it. They should be able to go and look and say, "Hey, I think this part could be better." (01:14:28): Or if they think we're biased, they should be able to work with the data and point it out. And if people have good observations, that should factor back into the code. And this is, again, something that's difficult to get people comfortable with, that everything is out there, you can't cover anything up. But I think that's so essential to people trusting it. Yeah, we set these out on day one. We go back to them constantly because we're always evolving the product, and we're always like got to make sure every new change is open. Whenever we update the scoring system, there's an update in GitHub when the data is published daily so you can download it. And so yeah, I think those have been really essential to the thing working.
turns.zh: 有一些原则，我觉得当我们最初把它们分享给公司里的人时，似乎可能有点疯狂。但我认为它们是产品奏效的原因，而且我认为它们一直非常重要，而我们确实如此。我们定期回到它们，今天、一直、总是。大概最疯狂的一条就是：这个东西将人民的声音。它将代表人民的声音。它不代表公司的声音。所以这不是一家科技公司在决定什么被展示。是人民在决定什么被展示，而那对设计有很多影响。首先，我们没有能改变一条注释状态的按钮。所以如果一条注释因为人们评分并觉得它有用而被展示，那它就会被展示。我们无法改变那个。(01:12:08)：而那是一种当我们最初提出时，会让人们不安的东西。他们会像“等等，所以某样东西能上去，而公司不能把它拿下来，或者不能改变它的状态、让它停止展示？”而我们就像“是的，而且它必须运作得那么好。如果它不够好到能做那个，那它就不work。”我们的关键原则之一是：如果一条注释有那么糟糕的问题，你想要对它做点什么，那其实是系统的问题。我们需要重新设计系统，让它展示好的注释。所以是的，我们得让每个人舒服地接受“没有按钮能改变一条注释的状态”这个想法。类似地，正如我们之前聊的，我们想让它代表全人类。(01:12:53)：所以我们不想做谁能进来当贡献者、谁不能的仲裁者。所以我们对它开放给每个人。你只需要满足一个非常基本的客观标准。你需要有一个经过验证的电话，以帮助减少机器人或类似东西参与的可能性。但除此之外，它是随机选择的，而且今天仍然如此。再说一次，人们花了一些时间才舒服地接受它。但我认为，这东西是人民的声音、并通过一个开放透明的流程反映他们的产出，这对它为什么好、为什么奏效、以及为什么被信任，都极其关键。所以那是第一点，而我觉得它将永远是产品的核心。另一个人们觉得疯狂的是透明。(01:13:49)：之前处理误导性信息的方式，对很多人来说，感觉像是黑箱——科技公司或媒体公司或领导层之类在做决定。我们就像“人们需要对此感到舒服。他们需要信任这个。所以整个东西必须公开。”决定哪些注释被分享的代码必须公开。让它发生的所有数据和评分必须公开。人们应该能拿走代码和数据，复现整个服务，并且我们确实做了我们说的我们做过的事。而且他们应该能审计它。他们应该能去查看并说“嘿，我觉得这部分可以更好。”(01:14:28)：或者如果他们觉得我们有偏见，他们应该能利用数据指出来。而如果人们有好的观察，那应该回馈进代码。而这也再次是那种很难让人们舒服接受的事——一切都摆在外面，你什么都掩盖不了。但我认为那对人们信任它太重要了。是的，我们在第一天就确立了这些。我们不断地回到它们，因为我们一直在演进产品，而我们总是“得确保每一个新改变都是开放的”。无论何时我们更新评分系统，GitHub 上都有一次更新，数据每天发布，所以你可以下载。所以是的，我觉得那些对这东西的成功真的不可或缺。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: And by the way, these do not come without a cost. It's actually really hard from an end perspective to actually open source the actual algorithm that's running on the actual data. Because the way large-scale services like this are usually architected does not naturally lend itself to being run as a script by someone who's downloaded a TSV. So we actually have to take weird architectural decisions to make this possible in a way that probably wouldn't have been if we didn't start with this assumption from scratch. We would've had to maybe rewrite the system to make it like this.
turns.zh: 而且顺便说，这些并非没有代价。从最终的角度，真的去开源那个运行在真实数据上的实际算法，其实非常难。因为这类大规模服务通常的架构方式，天然不适合被一个下载了 TSV 的人当作脚本跑起来。所以我们实际上得做奇怪的架构决策来让这成为可能，而如果我们不是从一开始就以这个假设从零开始，大概率不会是那样。我们大概得重写系统才能让它变成这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of that?
turns.zh: 能举个例子吗？

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: For instance, there's a matrix factorization that we train. Usually, you would train a matrix factor... train your ML model once and then serve it, I guess with a separate service. But we didn't want to have people externally spinning up services to be able to replicate the system that we had. So basically, I don't think it would've been actually very cool if we had open sourced the code in a way that wasn't actually runnable, I guess, by someone just... At this point, you can download Python code and run a script. You do need a lot of RAM right now, but you can do it on one machine.
turns.zh: 比如，有一个我们训练的矩阵分解。通常，你会训练一个矩阵分解……把你的 ML 模型训练一次然后服务它，我想是用一个独立的服务。但我们不想让外部的人为了复现我们拥有的系统而去拉起各种服务。所以基本上，我觉得如果以那种实际上不可被某人直接运行的方式去开源代码，其实一点都不酷，我猜——此刻，你可以下载 Python 代码并跑一个脚本。你现在确实需要大量 RAM，但你可以在一台机器上做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. How much RAM are we talking about?
turns.zh: 好的。你说的是多少 RAM？

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Oh, only like 500 gigs.
turns.zh: 哦，也就大概 500 G。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay. That's reasonable.
turns.zh: 好的。好的。那还合理。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: It'll take a day if you don't do anything special to speed it up. Good to know, but yeah.
turns.zh: 如果你不做任何加速的特殊处理，会花一天。知道这个也好，不过是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Possible is the key thing, and people have done it. Vitalik Buterin had a blog post where he talks about his explorations, making sure the algorithm really does what it says it does. And I think just the fact that a handful of people have done this, there's enough people who have done it that there's someone you'd probably trust who's verified it.
turns.zh: “可能”才是关键，而且人们确实做到了。Vitalik Buterin 有一篇博客文章，他讲述了自己的探索，确认这个算法确实做了它声称做的事。而我觉得，仅仅是已经有少数几个人这么做了——有够多的人做过，以至于有一个你大概会信任的人验证过它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's rolling out to Meta. No big deal. I love just as you described these principles, just I could imagine a PM at a company being like, "Okay, guys. Here, I want to do this project." There's so much idealism to it that rarely works in real life; going to be open source. You're going to give it to everyone. We don't have actual control over what it's going to do, don't worry about it. It's going to just change the way people see this thing that we've been very careful about and then it works. And I think that's very rare and it's really impressive. And what I'm hearing partly is that sticking to those principles was actually really fundamental to it working and not bending over when someone's like, "No, no, no, we can't do this. What if we change this part?"
turns.zh: 而且那正在推广到 Meta。小意思。我喜欢你描述这些原则的方式，就我能想象一家公司的 PM 像“好，兄弟们。这里，我想做这个项目。”里面有那么多理想主义，在真实生活里很少奏效：要开源。你要把它给每个人。我们对它能做什么没有实际控制，别担心。它会就那样改变人们看待我们一直很谨慎对待的这个东西的方式，然后它竟然奏效了。而我觉得那非常罕见，也真的令人印象深刻。而我部分听到的是，坚守那些原则实际上对它奏效真的根本，而当有人像“不不不，我们不能这么做。如果我们改这部分会怎样？”时，它没低头。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: I think if we had broken with any of those principles, if there was anything black box, if there was whatever, the product would be a lot harder to trust. And so I think it's because we've just stuck to them so cleanly simply that people can trust it.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果我们违背了其中任何一条原则，如果有任何黑箱、有任何什么，产品都会难信任得多。所以我认为，正是因为我们用这么干净、简单的方式坚守了它们，人们才能信任它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've talked about a few moments when it was like, wow, the White House changed their announcement because of the community note. We talked about the dog is a cat. Are there any other moments that after you launched of, "Holy shit, this is working? This is going to actually work."
turns.zh: 你聊过几个“哇”的时刻，比如白宫因为社区注释改了他们的公告。我们聊过狗是猫的事。在你们发布之后，还有没有什么别的“我靠，这真在奏效？这真要成了”的时刻？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: All along, we saw it working. We wanted to be confident whenever we expanded it to new audiences or new countries or whatever, we wanted to be confident it was going to work. So maybe held our breath a little bit just to see that it would do what we expected, but we always expected that. But that said, there were definitely stress cases. The one that comes to mind is the start of the Israel Hamas conflict in 2023 in October. That was probably the largest deluge of misleading information I've ever seen shared on the internet at one time. It was overwhelming. A number of photos and videos and whatever coming out related to that, it was insane. And just to give you an example, I think it was first three days or something of that conflict, we had 500 notes covering all sorts of different... out of context imagery. (01:19:32): Someone would say, "Hey, this is happening here." It's actually from 2013 in Syria. There were people making fake battle footage in the video game simulator Arma 3. So there were notes explaining, this stuff looked realistic. And unless you saw the note, you wouldn't really know. There are all sorts of claims about what was going on in the ground, and that was definitely... The product was still pretty new at that point. We'd expanded in the U. S. less than a year before that. We had been rolling out throughout the world that year and then this large event happened. And I felt like we were just enough prepared at the right time for the system to be able to handle that. (01:20:16): Probably one of the most important things we did right before that was launch the ability to write notes on images and videos and have those matched to other posts. I remember at that time thinking, "Wow, I'm glad we launched that feature a few months ago versus still had it on the shelf," because it was really important in that conflict. And I think even it was just a few weeks before we had launched a major speed up in notes too. When we first built the product, the number one focus was always quality. We knew that the product would live and die by the quality of the notes. That was the thing we could never give up on. We also knew it needed to deliver speed and scale, but we're like, "We will get the quality in the right place, and we can speed it up and scale-
turns.zh: 一直以来，我们都看到它在奏效。我们想在把它扩展到新受众、新国家等等时充满信心，我们想确信它会奏效。所以也许我们稍微屏住呼吸，只是想看看它会按我们预期的那样做，但我们一直都预期如此。话虽如此，确实有过压力测试。我想到的是 2023 年 10 月以色列-哈马斯冲突爆发。那大概是我见过的互联网上同时分享的误导性信息最大的一次洪流。它势不可挡。大量与此相关的照片、视频等等涌出来，简直疯狂。给你个例子，我想是冲突头三天左右，我们有 500 条注释覆盖了各种各样的……脱离语境的影像。(01:19:32)：有人会说“嘿，这发生在这里。”而它其实来自 2013 年的叙利亚。有人在用电子游戏模拟器 Arma 3 里制作假的战斗画面。所以有注释解释，这些东西看起来很真实。除非你看到那条注释，你不会真的知道。关于地面上在发生什么有各种说法，而那绝对……产品当时还相当新。我们在那之前不到一年才在美国扩展。那年我们一直在向全世界 roll out，然后这个大事件发生了。而我觉得我们刚好在正确的时间、刚好准备得足够，让系统能处理那个。(01:20:16)：我们之前做对的最重要的事之一，大概是上线了在图片和视频上写注释、并让它们匹配到其他帖子的能力。我记得当时我想“哇，我很高兴我们几个月前就上线了那个功能，而不是还把它搁在架子上”，因为它在那场冲突里真的很重要。而且我想甚至在那个冲突前几周，我们刚上线了一次注释速度的大幅提升。当我们最初打造产品时，第一焦点始终是质量。我们知道产品会因注释的质量而存亡。那是永远不能放弃的东西。我们也知道它需要交付速度和规模，但我们就像“我们会把质量放到正确的位置，而我们可以提速并扩展——”

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Get the quality in the right place and we can speed it up and scale it out over time. And we had actually just launched a speed-up that took three hours off the time it needed to go live, and it was I think a matter of weeks before that conflict happened, so again, super glad that was out there. In the first few days of the conflict the median time from a post going live to a note showing up was five hours, which is like crazy fast. Typical fact checking is like two to four, at least it's really common to see it take two to four days. These notes were showing up in five hours and we're like, we are so glad we got those things out before this happened, it made the service a lot more helpful.
turns.zh: 把质量放到正确的位置，而我们可以随着时间提速并扩展它。而我们其实刚上线了一个提速，把上线所需的时间砍掉了三个小时，而那场冲突发生前我想也就几周的事，所以再次，超级高兴那个已经在外面了。冲突头几天，从帖子上线到注释出现的中位时间是五小时，那快得离谱。典型的事实核查大概要两到四天，至少常见的是两到四天。这些注释在五小时内就出现了，而我们就像，我们太高兴在事情发生前就把那些东西发出去了，这让服务有用得多。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: One other thing that was, I think, nice to see working then was, one criticism of Community Notes some people bring up is, well if you always need agreement from people who typically disagree, then in these super polarized settings, that conflict being probably number one, then you wouldn't see any notes. But actually the reality was there were tons of notes about that conflict. So I think there was this kind of nice property where actually, and maybe this is a surprising fact, that there's more agreement out there across polarized divides than maybe conventional wisdom says, and the places where people agreed were really objectively true and verifiable. I guess maybe this is more true the more polarized the setting is, but where the agreement actually lends you, and basically notes that are very neutrally written, very focused on the facts and easy to verify information.
turns.zh: 当时看到奏效的另一个我觉得不错的事是，有些人对 Community Notes 的批评是：如果你总是需要那些通常意见相左的人的同意，那么在那些超级极化的环境里——那场冲突大概排第一——你就看不到任何注释了。但现实其实是，关于那场冲突有大量的注释。所以我觉得这里有个挺好的特性：实际上，也许这是个令人惊讶的事实，在极化分界线上方的共识，比传统智慧说的要多，而人们达成一致的地方，是真正客观上真实且可验证的。我猜也许环境越极化这越真实，但共识真正帮到你的地方，基本就是那些写得非常中立、非常聚焦事实、且容易验证信息的注释。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this talk for a while of just there's no more facts, nobody believes there is a single true fact anymore, everything is subjective, and I think Community Notes proves the opposite. Facts matter, there are facts that we can all agree with even on the most controversial topics.
turns.zh: 有段时间大家都在说“不再有事实了，没人相信还有单一的真实事实，一切都是主观的”，而我觉得 Community Notes 证明了相反的事。事实很重要，有些事实我们都能同意，即使是最有争议的话题。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, we saw this really from day one, when we would show those prototypes to people just depicting the idea, it was really obvious that people cared more about, or they cared a lot about understanding reality and what was going on and they were willing to disagree with their side, so to speak, to recognize that. And I think that's not always that obvious to people. The world does feel really polarized, but people definitely are willing to cross partisan boundaries to get to accurate information and that's why the product works.
turns.zh: 是的，我们从第一天起就真的看到了这个，当我们把那些描绘想法的原型展示给人们时，很明显人们更在乎、或非常在乎去理解现实和正在发生的事，而且他们愿意——可以说——不认同自己一方，去承认那个。而我觉得这对人们并不总是那么明显。世界确实感觉非常极化，但人们绝对愿意跨越党派界限去获取准确的信息，而那就是产品奏效的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like as we rely more and more on what we know and understand about the world is becoming social media online and moving this quickly, it's like I'm so thankful this exists because otherwise it'd just be, what do we trust anymore? This being out aligns with we need this thing to exist at the same time. And it feels like at the same time there's also people I just don't trust. I think people have shifted from I trust what I read to, okay, I shouldn't just believe everything I'm reading. Is there anything there you're noticing about just how people think about news they see and their shift of just like, I'm not going to believe everything. Is there anything that you've noticed about just human behavior or just the way we've shifted understanding what is true?
turns.zh: 感觉随着我们越来越依赖我们所知和理解的世界正在变成社交媒体线上、并且推进得这么快，我是如此感激它的存在，因为否则就只是，我们还能信任什么？它的出现与我们同时需要它存在是一致的。而且感觉同时也有些人我根本不信任。我觉得人们已经从“我信任我读到的”转向“好吧，我不该就相信我读到的一切”。关于人们如何看待他们看到的新闻、以及那种“我不会什么都信”的转变，你有没有注意到什么？关于人类行为、或我们理解何为真相的方式发生了怎样的转变，你有没有注意到什么？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: We haven't done any research to look broadly at how people's perceptions are changing there, but I certainly have found myself that particularly seeing notes, I am more skeptical about what I read at first, and I think that's been helpful. And we hear that from people, that they think about things a bit more, and I think that's a good secondary effect and benefit of something like this, which is the more you see the patterns of how what you're reading can be wrong, the more you can thoughtfully question it and try to get a better understanding of what's really going on. So historically I think this was called media literacy, but basic idea of can you understand the ways in which things can go wrong and try to cut them yourself.
turns.zh: 我们没做任何研究去广泛地看人们的认知在怎么变，但我自己确实发现，特别是看到注释后，我在一开始对读到的东西更怀疑了，而我觉得这很有帮助。我们也从人们那里听到，他们会对事情想得更多一点，而我觉得这是这类东西一个很好的次级效应和好处——你越是看到你读的东西可能出错的模式，你就越能深思熟虑地质疑它，并尝试更好地理解真正在发生什么。所以历史上我觉得这叫媒体素养，但基本理念是：你能不能理解事情可能出错的种种方式，并试着自己去剔除它们。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Another aspect I think we help with that is discovery of the Community Notes. I think often before Community Notes you could have just been living in a little news filter bubble, or maybe there were fact checks out there that you should have been reading but you weren't discovering them. So the fact that the note applies, it is directly attached to the post and visible by anyone who sees the post helps cross those filter bubbles and can kind of... I think for some people it's the first time they've actually seen counter arguments to claims made in their own little echo chamber.
turns.zh: 我认为我们帮助的另一个方面是社区注释的发现。我觉得在 Community Notes 之前，你可能只是生活在一个小小的新闻过滤气泡里，或者也许有一些你本该读的事实核查，但你没发现它们。所以当注释被加上时，它直接附在帖子上，任何看到帖子的人都能看见，这有助于跨越那些过滤气泡，并且可以说……对某些人来说，这是他们第一次真正看到对自己那个小回音室里所说说法的反驳论点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible, yeah. I love the point you're making about how it actually teaches people to be a little more skeptical of the things they read. It's an education system more than just, here, this one thing is wrong. I love that. (01:26:13): Okay, just a few more questions. There was an audience question asked on Twitter, we all asked on Twitter, "What do people want to know about Community Notes?" one was actually why you guys switched to anonymous contributors, what was the decision behind that?
turns.zh: 那太不可思议了，是的。我喜欢你提的这一点：它实际上在教导人们对读到的事更怀疑一点。它更像一种教育系统，而不只是“喏，这一件事是错的”。我喜欢那个。(01:26:13)：好，就几个问题了。Twitter 上有个观众提问，我们都在 Twitter 上问了，“关于 Community Notes 人们想知道什么？”其中一个其实是，你们为什么改成匿名贡献者，那背后的决定是什么？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, we had this pilot where we were testing with a small number of contributors, a few thousand contributors, and we learned a lot through that pilot. Probably the biggest thing we learned was related to anonymity or pseudonymity of contributors. We had originally assumed that it was important that people contribute under their real handle, or their real name, or whatever it was. The first prototypes depicted that, we kind of thought that would be important for people trusting the note, and actually it was totally wrong. The best option was actually opposite of what we first tried. (01:27:02): We found a few things. One, people were hesitant to write a note on a controversial topic because they didn't want to get attacked or harassed online. And so some people were comfortable doing this but others were not, and so it meant there was more potential good notes to be written than were getting written, and this was very clear feedback from the pilot. (01:27:24): Two, and this is super interesting, people are actually more willing to cross partisan boundaries when they are anonymous or pseudonymous than when they are under their real name, and it intuitively makes a lot of sense. If you publicly are using your name, you feel are affiliated with one side versus the other, you might hesitate to be perceived as breaking with that side. But you may actually, for example, find a note helpful that's critical of that side, and there's a bunch of studies that show when people are anonymous, they're much more willing to cross partisan boundaries and work with the other side, agree with the other side, and we saw that too. And so by allowing people to be pseudonymous, you actually get more honest answers about what they really think and it helps find disagreement that really-
turns.zh: 是的，我们有个试点，当时在用少量贡献者测试，几千个贡献者，而我们通过那个试点学到了很多。大概我们学到最大的事与贡献者的匿名或假名有关。我们原本假设人们用真实账号、真实姓名之类的来贡献很重要。第一版原型就是那么描绘的，我们有点觉得那对人们信任这条注释会很重要，而实际上完全错了。最好的选项其实和我们最初试的相反。(01:27:02)：我们发现了几件事。一，人们不愿意在一个有争议的话题上写注释，因为他们不想在网上被攻击或骚扰。所以有些人舒服做这个，但另一些不，这意味着本来能写的好注释比实际被写出来的更多，而那是试点里非常清晰的反馈。(01:27:24)：二，这个超级有趣，人们其实在匿名或假名时，比用真实姓名时更愿意跨越党派界限，而这在直觉上很讲得通。如果你公开用你的名字，你会觉得自己 affiliated with 某一方，你可能会犹豫被看作与那一方决裂。但你其实可能，比如，觉得一条批评那一方的注释有用，而且有一堆研究表明，当人们匿名时，他们更愿意跨越党派界限、与另一方合作、认同另一方，而我们也看到了这个。所以通过允许人们用假名，你实际上能得到更诚实的、关于他们真实想法的回答，而且它有助于找到真正——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so counterintuitive.
turns.zh: 那太反直觉了。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You never hear the opposite always, and it's so interesting it's the opposite.
turns.zh: 你从没听过相反的总是相反，而有趣的是它就是相反的。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: I think the same principle applies to making the likes private.
turns.zh: 我觉得同样的原则也适用于把点赞设为私密。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just thinking that.
turns.zh: 我刚在想那个。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I like a lot more stuff that's a little, definitely, I wouldn't have liked, yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，我会喜欢多得多那种有点……绝对，我本来不会点喜欢的东西，是的。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: It allows freedom for honesty, which is pretty great. And one of the criticisms of pseudonymity is it can generate, maybe people have reached the quality threshold that they put out there, but we have so many quality mechanisms in the system that that wasn't an issue, so we could keep quality high while opening up for that honesty.
turns.zh: 它给了诚实以自由，这相当棒。而对假名的一个批评是它可能产生——也许人们达到了他们放出去的质量门槛，但我们在系统里有这么多质量机制，那不是个问题，所以我们可以在为了那份诚实而开放的同时，保持高质量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another question, you touched on this a little bit, which is around navigating the existing trust and safety apparatus of Twitter, which as you described, basically, previously, it was like we make decisions on what is true and not, and every company works this way, you guys basically upended that like, here's a completely different way, you have no control over what we say is true or not. Talk about just that experience of overcoming that, I imagine, very difficult hurdle of like, okay, forget all that, we're going to do it totally different.
turns.zh: 另一个问题，你稍微提到过，是关于如何 navigate Twitter 既有的信任与安全机制——正如你描述的，基本上以前是“我们对什么是真什么不是做决定”，而每家公司都这么运作，你们基本上颠覆了那个——比如，这里是个完全不同的方式，你们对我们说什么是真什么不是没有控制。聊聊克服那个的经历，我想象，那是个非常困难的障碍，就像“好，忘了所有那些，我们要完全不一样地做”。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Yeah, it was definitely, what we were proposing was very different. I will say that I think people were sort of open-minded to it, generally speaking, and I think everyone had a sense that what was being done at the time wasn't really working that well or solving the problem, and people were open to new ideas, so that's a good foundation. (01:29:39): But I think one thing we did that was probably very helpful in that is we wanted the product to prove itself at any point. First it had to prove that people could possibly find notes helpful, then it had to prove that people could possibly write these notes that would be good quality. And so anytime that we were proposing doing something with the product, like running some research test, or running the pilot, or expanding the pilot, we always had the data that had convinced us that that was a good decision, like we were stepping into the next phase of expansion that made sense. And so I think we probably rarely proposed anything that seemed unwise, because we were holding such a high bar for quality ourselves, and I suspect that went a long way.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对，我们当时提的方案非常不同。我想说，总体而言，我觉得人们对其相当开放，而且我想每个人都有种感觉，当时在做的东西其实并没有真的运作得很好或解决问题，而人们对新想法是开放的，所以那是个好基础。(01:29:39)：但我觉得我们做的一件在那个过程中可能非常有帮助的事，是我们想让产品在任何节点都证明自己。首先它得证明人们可能觉得注释有用，然后它得证明人们可能写出这些高质量的注释。所以无论何时我们提议用产品做点什么——比如跑某个研究测试、或者跑试点、或者扩展试点——我们总是有数据说服我们自己那是个好决定，就像我们正迈入下一个说得通的扩展阶段。所以我觉得我们大概很少提议任何显得不明智的事，因为我们自己就维持着这么高的质量标准，而我想那起了很大作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's partly, what I'm hearing is, take it step by step to prove this is actually working, and partly be confident it is working to yourself before you try to convince the trust and safety team this is the way to go.
turns.zh: 所以部分是，我听到的是，一步一步来，证明这真的在奏效，部分是在你试图说服信任与安全团队这是该走的路之前，先对自己确信它确实在奏效。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was there a moment along that journey it shifted from no way this is a thing to okay, wow, let's actually consider this? Or was it this very gradual process?
turns.zh: 在那段旅程里，有没有某个时刻，它从“绝不可能这东西能成”转变为“好吧，哇，我们真得考虑这个了”？还是说这是个非常渐进的过程？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Whether other people were saying no way to wow, let's actually-
turns.zh: 无论别人是从“绝不可能”到“哇，我们真得——”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, just internally of just like, okay, we're going to actually stop this trust and safety way of operating and instead rely on Community Notes, was there a moment of like, okay, let's actually make that switch, or was that Elon actually, is that the big switch?
turns.zh: 是的，就内部而言，就像“好，我们要真的停止这种信任与安全的运作方式，转而依赖 Community Notes”，有没有某个“好，我们真要做那个切换”的时刻，还是说那是 Elon 真正——那是那个大切换？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: The biggest change there happened in X, the biggest changes prior to that were just the decision to put this out there and have it be operating in public at first US wide scale. But yeah, then the bigger switches came in the X period.
turns.zh: 那里最大的变化发生在 X 时期，而那之前最大的变化，只是决定把它放出去、并让它以最初的全美规模公开运营。但是的，然后更大的切换是在 X 时期到来的。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: I think even though there was original research before Birdwatch had even started, or Community Notes had even started, from external researchers showing that crowdsourced fact-checkers, laypeople can do about as well as fact-checkers and actually the agreement rates were kind of similar between the groups. I think even though that research was out there, I think there were definitely a lot of people who didn't really believe it could work until it already worked.
turns.zh: 我觉得即使早在 Birdwatch 甚至 Community Notes 还没开始之前，就有外部研究者的原始研究，表明众包的事实核查员、外行，能做得和专业事实核查员差不多好，而且实际上两组之间的共识率差不多类似。我觉得即使那研究已经存在，肯定还是有很多人直到它真的奏效了才真正相信它能行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically prove it, prove that it works. Yeah, that makes sense, versus just a bunch of docs and strategy and thinking, it's just like, look, it's actually working, you can see for yourself.
turns.zh: 基本上证明它，证明它奏效。是的，那讲得通，而不是只是一堆文档、战略和想法，就像“看，它真的在奏效，你自己能看到”。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. Okay, possibly last question, we'll see which fractals of questions you guys bring up here. I referenced this a couple times, this incredible achievement of keeping a project alive through Jack and then, I have this note, and Kayvon running the show then, and then Parag running Twitter, and then Elon, and then Linda taking over as CEO, quite rare, especially something this visible, this impactful to everything that X is. Any lessons or keys to that actually working, of this project surviving throughout so many work changes and leaders?
turns.zh: 讲得通。好，可能是最后一个问题，我们看看你们在这里会引申出什么分形的问题。我提过几次这个，这个了不起的成就：让一个项目在 Jack、然后（我有这个笔记）Kayvon 掌舵、然后 Parag 运营 Twitter、然后 Elon、然后 Linda 接任 CEO 期间都存活下来，相当罕见，尤其对一个这么显眼、对 X 的一切都这么有影响力的东西。关于它真的成功、这个项目在这么多工作变动和领导层之下存活下来，有任何经验教训或关键吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: It definitely has been a crazy time to be building something. It's been fun. The craziness has been entertaining. I think one reason perhaps the product has done so well and survived is the nature of the product itself. It is designed to produce information that is found helpful by people who normally disagree. And so even if you have CEOs or leaders who might disagree, there's a good chance actually they'll find it helpful, they'll be like, wow, this thing does produce pretty useful output. So I think there's something in the nature of the product itself, that when people see it, whatever side they're on, left, up, down, they're likely to find it pretty helpful, so I do think that helps. (01:33:39): I also think the team executed really well. We had ambitious goals that were exciting, they solved a real problem. This is a real problem that matters in the world. At every step, as we talked about, the product needed to prove itself, and we would make sure it proved itself and we would bring the results that convinced us and we'd share those with people. And so they would say, oh yeah, I agree, it kind of proved itself, let's take the next leap. And we've done that all along the way and we continue to operate that way, and I think that focus on the outcome and goal that matters, and executing against it, really helped. (01:34:24): The team did not get distracted by much all through the period during which the acquisition happened. There was a lot of opportunity for distraction. This team was shipping every week, we were super focused on the goal, let's make this thing work, let's get these notes out there, and I think people saw that execution and were excited to support it.
turns.zh: 做东西的这段时间绝对疯狂。也很有趣。那种疯狂挺有意思。我觉得产品做得这么好并存活下来的一个原因，也许是产品本身的性质。它被设计成产出那些通常被意见相左的人觉得有用的信息。所以即使你有的 CEO 或领导可能意见不同，很有可能他们其实会觉得它有用，他们会像“哇，这东西确实产出相当有用的产出”。所以我觉得产品本身的性质里有点什么——当人们看到它，无论他们站在哪一边，左、上、下，他们很可能觉得它相当有用，所以我确实觉得那有帮助。(01:33:39)：我也觉得团队执行得真的很好。我们有激动人心的宏大目标，它们解决了一个真实的问题。这是个世界上重要的真实问题。正如我们聊的，每一步，产品都需要证明自己，而我们会确保它证明自己，我们会带来说服了我们自己的结果，并分享给人们。于是他们会说，哦对，我同意，它确实证明了自己，我们迈向下一个跳跃吧。我们一路都这么做，并继续以那种方式运作，而我觉得那种对重要结果和目标的聚焦、以及对照它执行，真的很有帮助。(01:34:24)：在收购发生的那段时期，团队没被太多事分心。有很多分心的机会。这个团队每周都在发布，我们超级聚焦于目标——让这个东西奏效，把这些注释发出去，而我觉得人们看到了那种执行，并兴奋地支持它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, like it's working, why would we mess with that? And it's important, and it keeps us from having to hire tens of thousands of people to fact check.
turns.zh: 是的，就像它在奏效，我们为什么要去搞砸它？而且它重要，它让我们不用去雇数以万计的人来做事实核查。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: The interesting thing about that is no one ever asked us or brought up or seemed to care about anything related to cost savings in this process. And I think that's an assumption people have outside the company, that this must have been a reason there was interest in it. But that was never a goal, it was not at all why the project was started, it was not why people were excited about the project. And I think that's also, for people outside who maybe don't see the conversations, it's kind of a heartening thing to know, is that the focus was always on solving the problem. The other approach is even if you had 10,000 people doing it, the real issue is that they don't work that well because they're not trusted or they don't scale or they're too slow. And so the goal was really always just help people stay informed at scale. Let's build an internet scale solution to an internet scale problem that people like.
turns.zh: 关于那个有趣的事是，从没人问过我们、提起过、或似乎关心过这个过程中任何与成本节约相关的东西。而我觉得那是公司外的人有的一个假设，认为这一定是人们对其感兴趣的原因。但那从来不是个目标，完全不是项目启动的原因，也不是人们对此兴奋的原因。而我觉得那对外部那些也许没看到那些对话的人来说，也是个挺鼓舞人心的事——焦点始终在解决问题上。另一种做法是，即使你有一万人做这个，真正的问题在于他们做得并不够好，因为他们不被信任、或不能规模化、或太慢。所以目标真的始终是帮助人们在规模上保持知情。我们来构建一个互联网规模的解决方案，去解决一个人们喜欢的、互联网规模的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I heard about you, Keith, when I was asking people about how this worked and why this worked so well is that they describe you with having a very low ego, and that allowed you to give up this whole team and power and influence and just the name, forget it, whatever you want, we'll call it Community Notes, great. Is there anything in there you can share of just how you think about that and how important that is as a product leader to have a low ego?
turns.zh: 我听到的关于你的一件事，Keith，当我就“这怎么运作、为什么运作这么好”问别人时，他们把你描述成有着非常低的 ego（自我），那让你能放弃整个团队、权力和影响力，还有名字，去他的，你想叫什么都行，我们就叫它 Community Notes，很好。关于你如何看待那个、以及作为一个产品负责人，低 ego 有多重要，你有什么能分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: For me, this project, I feel like I get to do community service with this project. I see my work as in service of the people and the community, and that's what motivates me. The only thing that I care about is delivering the outcome that the world finds helpful. And so in some ways the project has not been about ego, it's about truth-seeking, let's find... Not truth in the sense of what information is true, but let's find out what's actually going to make this work. How does it need to be structured, what should it be called? Whatever is going to produce the best outcome is what we should do. So I think I feel more attached to the product being helpful than to anything else, and so to whatever degree it might seem like low ego is probably more a result of wanting to actually solve the problem.
turns.zh: 对我来说，这个项目，我觉得我是在通过这个项目做社区服务。我把自己的工作看作是为人民和社区服务，而那正是激励我的东西。我唯一在乎的，是交付出世界觉得有帮助的结果。所以在某些方面，这个项目从来不是关于 ego，它是关于求真的——不是“什么信息为真”意义上的真理，而是让我们搞清楚什么真的会让它奏效。它该被怎么搭建，它该叫什么？无论什么能产生最好的结果，我们就该那么做。所以我觉得我更依附于“产品有用”这件事，胜过其他任何东西，所以无论看起来低 ego 到什么程度，大概更多是想要真正解决问题的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think partly what I'm hearing is just if you win and succeed, good things will happen, so focus on that.
turns.zh: 而我觉得部分我听到的是，就是如果你赢了、成功了，好事就会发生，所以聚焦在那个上。

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: Certainly satisfying things will happen, it's very satisfying to have people appreciate it. It's satisfying that people on the left and right love it. It's satisfying that even people who receive notes, love notes, and reach out to them and post them, that's amazing, it feels so good to have helped give people that, and yeah, it's very motivating. It's a great reason to wake up in the morning.
turns.zh: 当然满足感的东西会发生，被人们欣赏非常满足。左派和右派的人都爱它，让人满足。连收到注释的人、爱注释的人、主动联系他们并转发它们，都让人惊叹，帮人们得到那个感觉太好了，是的，那非常激励人。那是早上醒来的一个很好的理由。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's absurd this has worked, but it's also like of course this would work, of course something like this should work. It's like such interesting-
turns.zh: 这能成简直荒谬，但它也像“当然这能成，当然这种东西就该成”。这太有趣了——

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: It's the internet, it's of the internet, that's why it works.
turns.zh: 它是互联网，它来自互联网，那就是它为什么奏效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Where's Community Notes going from here? What's happening, where's it going, what's the future?
turns.zh: 哦天哪。Community Notes 接下来要去哪？在发生什么，要去哪，未来是什么？

turns.speaker: Keith Coleman
turns.en: We're always working on basically more better notes faster. So there's clearly an opportunity to get more notes out there, we want them to stay as good or better than they are, we want to get them there faster, so we're always working on core product changes to help deliver that. Recently, for example, we just released an update to what we call the Community Notes bat signal, or the ability to request a Community Note. So anyone on X can say, "Hey, I think this post needs a Community Note," and now they can even add a source explaining why so that when a prospective writer sees that it's much easier for them to write a note. So we're always working on core things like that, core algorithm improvements. (01:38:47): I think there are also new frontiers that show a lot of potential, AI and LLMs are one. It's easy to imagine a lot of ways that AI could assist the people in this task they're doing of trying to get information out there quickly. And maybe Jay should talk about the Supernotes work that we've done with some folks outside the company.
turns.zh: 我们一直在做的，基本就是更多、更好、更快的注释。所以显然有机会让更多注释出去，我们希望它们保持和现在一样好甚至更好，我们希望更快地让它们到位，所以我们一直在做核心产品改动来帮助交付那个。比如最近，我们刚发布了一个我们叫 Community Notes“蝙蝠信号”（bat signal）的更新，或者说请求一条 Community Note 的能力。所以 X 上的任何人都可以说“嘿，我觉得这条帖子需要一条 Community Note”，而现在他们甚至可以加一个来源解释为什么，这样当一个潜在的写作者看到时，写注释对他们就容易多了。所以我们一直在做像那样的核心事务、核心算法改进。(01:38:47)：我觉得也有展现很大潜力的新前沿，AI 和 LLM 是其中之一。很容易想象 AI 能在很多方面辅助人们做这个“尽快把信息发出去”的任务。也许 Jay 应该聊聊我们和公司外一些人做的 Supernotes 工作。

turns.speaker: Jay Baxter
turns.en: Yeah, so one cool thing about having public data and code is that external researchers can collaborate with you, and in this case Supernotes had this idea that we can basically take existing notes as input, existing proposed notes that maybe they have some problem, maybe they have part of the story, maybe they're worded in kind of a biased way. Basically take all these in, have an LLM generate a ton of different variants, and then basically make the simulated jury to basically get a representative group of contributors for community notes who would be rating the note and try to predict based on their past ratings how they would rate these LLM generated notes. And so this way you can actually, rather than just having an LLM write a note from scratch and hoping it's good, you can simulate the entire community notes rating process and explicitly create notes that are likely to be rated helpful by people. (01:40:18): So I think ideas like that are very promising for the future, and it's a nice way that LLMs and humans can work together. Obviously agents can browse the web too, and that's one way that you could imagine agents assisting humans is maybe checking whether a note is actually supported by the source. Although then you get into things like, well, are people going to actually be as diligent? Right now I think raters are very diligent because they know just some Community Notes contributor wrote this like, I better check this before I rate it helpful. But hopefully we can design things in a way such that people don't trust the output and actually verify it themselves before issuing a helpful rating.
turns.zh: 是的，所以拥有公开的数据和代码的一个很酷的事，是外部研究者能和你协作，而在这个 case 里 Supernotes 有个想法：我们基本可以把现存的注释作为输入，那些现存的、也许有些问题的提议注释——也许它们只有部分故事，也许措辞有点偏见。基本把所有这些都放进去，让一个 LLM 生成大量不同的变体，然后基本造一个模拟的评审团，基本找一群有代表性的 Community Notes 贡献者——他们本来会给注释评分——并基于他们过去的评分，尝试预测他们会怎么给这些 LLM 生成的注释打分。所以这样你实际上可以，不是只让 LLM 从零写一条注释并指望它好，而是可以模拟整个 Community Notes 的评分过程，并明确地创造出那些很可能被人评为有帮助的注释。(01:40:18)：所以我觉得像那样的想法对未来的前景很好，而且它是 LLM 和人类能协作的一个好方式。显然 agent 也能浏览网页，而那是一种你可以想象 agent 辅助人类的方式——比如检查一条注释是否真的被那个来源支持。虽然那样你就进入了一些问题，比如，人们真的会那么勤勉吗？现在我觉得评分者非常勤勉，因为他们知道只是某个 Community Notes 贡献者写了这个，我最好在评它有助之前检查一下。但希望我们能以某种方式设计，让人们不信任输出、而是在给出“有帮助”评分前自己验证它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that is such an interesting area to explore where you want to avoid AI hallucinating slop versus make it easier and scale it even further. What an interesting challenge.
turns.zh: 是的，那是个非常有趣的探索领域，你想避免 AI 产生幻觉垃圾、又想让它更容易、进一步规模化。多有趣的挑战。

turns.en: What's cool about this project, in addition to the AI element, is that it's being done outside the company. We talked earlier about the open source transparency. The key reason we made this all open source was so people could see how it worked, but the dream is actually that, it's not just that the contributions to the notes and ratings are from the people, but the dream is actually the product is built by the people. What if the scoring algorithm were significantly or entirely written by the public? That would be incredible. And Supernotes is probably the first very substantial potential change in the algorithm of the way it works, that was kind of coming from the outside and plausibly could be part of the core, so we'd love to see the product go in that direction as well.
turns.zh: 这个项目酷的地方，除了 AI 元素，是它是在公司外部被做的。我们之前聊过开源透明。我们把这一切开源的关键原因，是让人们能看到它怎么运作，但梦想其实是，不只是注释和评分的贡献来自人民，梦想其实是产品是由人民造的。如果评分算法显著地、或完全由公众来写会怎样？那会不可思议。而 Supernotes 大概是第一个非常实质性的、可能改变它运作方式算法的潜在改动，它来自外部，并可能合理地成为核心的一部分，所以我们也乐于看到产品往那个方向走。

turns.en: Sweet, go Supernotes. Well guys, the work you're doing is tremendous. This is every product person's dream, I think to work, on something like this. Small team, lots of support, lots of impact, just innately interesting, and so I think this is going to inspire a lot of people. (01:42:27): So let me just ask you, is there anything else you wanted to share? Anything else you think might be helpful for folks to leave them with?
turns.zh: 甜，去吧 Supernotes。好家伙，你们做的工作是巨大的。我觉得这是每个产品人的梦想，能在这样的东西上工作。小团队，大量支持，大量影响力，本身就极其有趣，所以我觉得这会激励很多人。(01:42:27)：所以让我就问你们，还有什么你们想分享的吗？你们觉得有什么别的、可能有助于留给人们的东西？

turns.en: Sure, I guess one thing that just I thought was interesting over the course of working on this product is just there's... I think in a similar way to how retweets originally were not something Jack came up with, I think users just started doing it and then it became a core part of the product. So I think that's just another dimension in which commuted notes is a product that's driven by the people.
turns.zh: 当然，我想有一件事，在开发这个产品的过程中我觉得很有趣，就是……我觉得类似于转发（retweet）最初不是 Jack 想出来的——我想是用户自己开始那么做，然后它成了产品的核心部分。已经有一个很大的方面，就是有很多我们真的没预期到的、人们想用 Community Notes 做的事，而看到那些用户需求浮现很酷。(01:43:04)：我想一个例子，我们一直想象的是政治类的虚假信息，但出于某种原因，有很多人爱辩论 Messi（梅西）还是 Ronaldo（C罗）进球更多。我猜那是个有点好笑的。还有一个社区审核的方面，所以我想我们也曾以为这专门是用来给误导性或潜在误导性信息补充背景，但你能看到的是，有些注释超出了那个，去点名他们认为 spam 或类似的内容。所以我觉得那是 Community Notes 作为一个由人民驱动的产品、的又一个维度。

turns.en: Yeah, community Notes is cool itself, but I think what it points to about society is actually even bigger. (01:45:23): And I think that's a really big reason for optimism about the world, is that while it might feel polarized, there's probably like an 80% set of people that agree on quite a lot of things. turns.zh: 是的，Community Notes 本身很酷，但我觉得它指向的关于社会的事其实更大。社会经常感觉真的极化，你总是听到人们聊这个，没人能在任何事上达成一致，但实际上 Community Notes 向你展示了人们确实能在相当多的事上达成一致。即使在与政治等相关的超级有争议的话题上，也有大量共识，那就是注释为什么奏效。(01:45:23)：而我觉得那是对世界乐观的一个很大理由——虽然它感觉极化，但大概有 80% 的人在很多事上达成一致。想象一下，如果我们能用我们在注释上用的同样的方法，去找到关于立法、政策、或人们希望政府或世界去做的类似事情的共识，我们也许能在那些人们真正想要的想法上获得大得多的势能，而大家都会开心得多。也许边缘上 10% 的人不会开心，但我打赌有很多我们没识别出的共识，而如果我们做了，我们都会相当开心。所以我不知道，我觉得人们很容易对世界感到悲观，但我觉得这个产品是乐观看待未来的一个好理由。
